Section 1
Introduction

        The COBOL source language implemented by the Universal Compiling System (UCS)
        COBOL, commonly known as UCOB, includes all required features of the American
        National Standards Institute (ANSI) COBOL X3.23ΓÇô1985 and of the Federal Information
        Processing Standards Publication 21ΓÇô2 (FIPS PUB 21ΓÇô2). In addition, it includes
        numerous compatibility features for migration from ASCII COBOL to UCS COBOL.

        The UCS COBOL compiler uses the ASCII and ISO character sets in processing source
        text and object time character data. The compiler is fully reentrant and produces
        optimized reentrant code usable in multibanked, common-banked, or transaction
        program environments.


1.1. About this Manual
Purpose
        This manual provides instruction in using the Universal Compiling System (UCS)
        COBOL, commonly known as UCOB, on OS 2200 systems. UCS COBOL generates
        code for execution in extended mode on 2200 Series systems.

Scope
        UCS COBOL includes all required features of the American National Standards Institute
        (ANSI) COBOL X3.23ΓÇô1985 and FIPS PUB 21ΓÇô2 (Federal Information Processing
        Standards Publication 21ΓÇô2). In addition, it includes numerous compatibility features for
        migration from ASCII COBOL to UCS COBOL.

Audience
        This manual is intended for systems and applications programmers and analysts who
        are already familiar with the COBOL programming language.

Prerequisites
        To use this manual effectively, you should have knowledge of the UCS COBOL
        programming language as well as familiarity with basic OS 2200 job control language
        concepts.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                 1ΓÇô1
Introduction




Notations Conventions
        This manual uses the following conventions to illustrate COBOL syntax:

        UPPERCASE represents COBOL keywords that are required in the syntax. Keywords
        must be spelled exactly as shown.

        UPPERCASE in brackets represents keywords that you can optionally use to make
        your program more readable. Keywords must be spelled exactly as shown.

        italic lowercase represents terms such as

        ΓÇó    UCS COBOL words
        ΓÇó    Literals
        ΓÇó    PICTURE character strings
        ΓÇó    Comment entries
        ΓÇó    Complete syntactical entries that you supply

        Where a term may be repeated in a general format, a number is appended to the term
        to identify that term for explanation or discussion (for example, identifier ΓÇô1).

        []
        indicate a choice of one or more of the enclosed options that can either be specified
        or omitted.

        {}
        indicate a choice of one or more of the enclosed options. Unlike options enclosed in
        brackets, you must explicitly or implicitly specify one of the options enclosed in
        braces.

        represents the omission of a word or words, generally to illustrate that portions of
        syntax can be repeated.

        01, 02,...77 or level-number

        represent specific level numbers that are required for the data description formats in
        which they appear. If a specific level is not identified, level-number is specified and the
        legal level numbers are explained in the rules for the format.

        separators

        include the comma, semicolon, and space. These separators are interchangeable
        within your source program; however, you must use the separator period when it is
        used in formats.




1ΓÇô2                                                                                7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                                  Introduction




        special character words

        such as +, ΓÇô, < , > , and =, must be specified when using portions of formats that
        contain them.


1.2. Documentation Updates
        This document contains all the information that was available at the time of
        publication. Changes identified after release of this document are included in problem

1.3. COBOL X3.23ΓÇô1974,ΓÇô1985 Differences
     Potentially Not Affecting Existing Programs
        The COBOL 85 standard contains many new features that were not in COBOL 74 and
        should not have any impact on existing programs. These new features include new
        verbs as well as additional capabilities for existing verbs. The following is a list of
        changes of substance included in the COBOL 85 standard:

        ΓÇó   Lowercase letters
            When the computer character set includes lowercase letters, they can be used in
            character strings. Except when used in nonnumeric literals, each is equivalent to
            the corresponding uppercase letter.
        ΓÇó   Colon (:) character
            The COBOL character set has been expanded to include the colon (:) character that
            is used in reference modification.
        ΓÇó   Punctuation characters
            The separators comma, semicolon, and space are interchangeable within a source
            program.
        ΓÇó   User-defined words and system names
            The same COBOL word can be used as a system name and as a user-defined
            word within a source program; the context in which a COBOL word occurs
            determines what it is.
        ΓÇó   Symbolic characters
            A symbolic character is a user-defined word that specifies a user-defined
            figurative constant.
        ΓÇó   Nonnumeric literal
            A nonnumeric literal has an upper limit of 160 characters in length. The upper limit
            was 120 characters in the COBOL 74 standard.
        ΓÇó   Figurative constant ZERO
            The figurative constant ZERO is allowed in arithmetic expressions.


7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                1ΓÇô3
Introduction




        ΓÇó   Uniqueness of reference
            A user-defined word need not be unique or be capable of being made unique
            unless referenced.
        ΓÇó   Qualification
            An implementor must provide the capability to handle 50 levels of qualification.
            Five levels of qualification were required in the COBOL 74 standard.
        ΓÇó   Subscripting
            A table can have up to seven dimensions. Up to 3 dimensions were allowed in the
            COBOL 74 standard.
        ΓÇó   Relative subscripting
            Relative subscripting allows a subscript to be followed by the operator + or ΓÇô,
            which is followed by an integer.
        ΓÇó   Mixing subscripts and indexes
            Indexes and data-name subscripts can both be written in a single set of subscripts
            used to reference an individual occurrence of a multidimensional table.
        ΓÇó   Reference modification
            Reference modification is a new method of referencing data by specifying a
            leftmost character and length for the data item.
        ΓÇó   Sequence number
            The sequence number can contain any character in the computerΓÇÖs character set.
            In COBOL 74 the sequence number contained only digits.
        ΓÇó   Data Division reference format
            The word following a level indicator, level number 01, or level number on the same
            line can begin in area A.
        ΓÇó   End program header
            The end program header indicates the end of the named COBOL source program.
        ΓÇó   Nested source programs
            Programs can be contained in other programs.
        ΓÇó   INITIAL clause in PROGRAM-ID
            The INITIAL clause specifies a program whose state is initialized, whenever the
            program is called, to the same state as when that program was first called in the
            run unit.
        ΓÇó   COMMON clause in PROGRAM-ID
            The COMMON clause specifies a program that, despite being directly contained
            within another program, can be called from any program directly or indirectly
            contained in that other program.
        ΓÇó   Environment Division
            The Environment Division is optional.




1ΓÇô4                                                                             7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                                 Introduction




        ΓÇó   SPECIALΓÇôNAMES paragraph
            If implementor name is a switch, condition name need not be a switch.
        ΓÇó   SPECIALΓÇôNAMES paragraph
            The reserved word IS has been made optional in the SPECIALΓÇôNAMES paragraph
            to be consistent with the use of IS throughout the COBOL language.
        ΓÇó   STANDARDΓÇô2 option
            The STANDARDΓÇô2 option within the ALPHABET clause of the SPECIALΓÇôNAMES
            paragraph allows the specification of the ISO 7ΓÇôbit character set for a character
            code set or collating sequence.
        ΓÇó   ASSIGN clause
            A nonnumeric literal can be specified in the ASSIGN clause.
        ΓÇó   OPTIONAL phrase
            The OPTIONAL phrase within the file control entry applies to sequential files,
            relative files and indexed files opened in the input, IΓÇôO, or extend mode.
        ΓÇó   ORGANIZATION clause
            Within the ORGANIZATION clause of the file control entry, the words
            ORGANIZATION IS have been made optional.
        ΓÇó   PADDING CHARACTER clause
            The PADDING CHARACTER clause in the file control entry specifies the character
            that is to be used for block padding on sequential files.
        ΓÇó   RECORD DELIMITER clause
            The RECORD DELIMITER clause in the file control entry indicates the method of
            determining the length of a variable length record.
        ΓÇó   IΓÇôOΓÇôCONTROL paragraph
            The order of clauses is immaterial in the IΓÇôOΓÇôCONTROL paragraph.
        ΓÇó   Data Division
            The Data Division is optional.
        ΓÇó   BLOCK CONTAINS clause
            Omission of the BLOCK CONTAINS clause is permitted if the number of records
            contained in a block is specified by the operating environment.
        ΓÇó   CODEΓÇôSET clause
            The CODEΓÇôSET clause can be specified for all files with sequential organization.
        ΓÇó   LABEL RECORDS clause
            The LABEL RECORDS clause is optional; if not specified, then the clause LABEL
            RECORDS ARE STANDARD is assumed.
        ΓÇó   LINAGE clause
            Data names within the LINAGE clause can be qualified.

1.4. COBOL X3.23ΓÇô1974,ΓÇô1985 Differences
     Potentially Affecting Existing Programs
        The COBOL 85 standard contains some new features that were not in COBOL 74 that
        could have an impact on existing programs. For a complete list and discussion of
        changes that have a potential impact on migration from ASCII COBOL, refer to Volume
        2, Appendix E.

Section 2
Programming Considerations


2.1. General
        0055CS COBOL offers many features that allow you to obtain a necessary function
        without programming the function in detail. For information on programming in detail,
        see the appropriate section for specific information. This section provides general
        information about various language concepts.


2.2. Files
        A file is a collection of records that can be placed into or retrieved from a storage
        medium. You can choose the file organization and the file processing method and
        sequence. Although the file organization and processing method are restricted for
        sequential media, no such restrictions exist for mass storage media.

        When describing the capabilities of UCS COBOL programs to manipulate files, the
        following conventions are used:

        ΓÇó   The term ΓÇ£file nameΓÇ¥ means the user-defined word used in the UCS COBOL
            source program to refer to a file.
        ΓÇó   The terms ΓÇ£file referred to by file nameΓÇ¥ and ΓÇ£fileΓÇ¥ mean the physical file
            regardless of the file name used in the COBOL program.
        ΓÇó   The term ΓÇ£file connectorΓÇ¥ means the entity containing information concerning the
            file.
        ΓÇó   All accesses to physical files occur through file connectors.

2.2.1. File Attributes
        A file has several attributes that apply to the file at the time it is created and cannot be
        changed during the lifetime of the file. The primary attribute is the organization of the
        file, which describes its logical structure. There are three organizations: sequential,
        relative, and indexed. Other fixed attributes of the file provided by the UCS COBOL
        program are prime record key, alternate record keys, code set, the minimum and
        maximum logical record size, the record type (fixed or variable), the collating sequence
        of the keys for indexed files, the blocking factor, the padding character, and the record
        delimiter.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                   2ΓÇô1
Programming Considerations




        A logical record is the unit of data that is retrieved from or stored in a file. The number
        of records that can exist in a file is limited only by the capacity of the storage media.

        There are two types of records: fixed length and variable length. When a file is
        created, it is declared to contain either fixed-length or variable-length records.

        In either case, the content of the record area does not reflect any control information
        added to the record on the physical storage medium (such as record length headers),
        nor does the length of the record you use reflect these additions.

2.2.2. File Processing
        A file can be processed by performing operations on individual records or on the file
        as a unit. Unusual conditions that occur during processing are communicated back to
        the program.

Record Operations
        The ACCESS MODE clause of the file control entry specifies the manner in which the
        object program operates on records within a file. The access mode can be sequential,
        random, or dynamic.

        For files that are organized as relative or indexed, any of the three access modes can
        be used to access the file regardless of the access mode used to create the file. A file
        with sequential organization can be accessed in sequential mode only.

        Open Mode
        The open mode of the file is related to the actions to be performed on records in the
        file and is specified in the OPEN statement. The open modes and purposes are:

        ΓÇó   Input to retrieve records
        ΓÇó   Output to place records into a file
        ΓÇó   Extend to append records to an existing file
        ΓÇó   I-O to retrieve and update records

        When the open mode is input, a file can be accessed by the READ statement. The
        START statement can also be used for files organized as indexed or relative that is in
        sequential or dynamic access modes.

        When the open mode is output, the records are placed into the file by issuing WRITE,
        GENERATE, or TERMINATE statements.

        When the open mode is extended, new records are added to the logical end of a file
        by issuing WRITE statements.




2ΓÇô2                                                                                7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                              Programming Considerations




        Only mass storage files can be referred to in the open IΓÇôO mode. The additional
        capabilities of mass storage devices permit updating in place, therefore READ and
        REWRITE statements can always be used. A mass storage file can be updated in the
        same manner as a file on a sequential medium by transcribing the entire file into
        another file (perhaps in a separate area of mass storage) using READ and WRITE
        statements. However, it is sometimes more efficient to update a mass storage file in
        place. This mass storage file maintenance technique uses the REWRITE statement to
        return to their previous locations on the storage medium only those records that have
        changed. READ and REWRITE statements are the only operations allowed while
        updating in place sequentially organized files.

        However, for indexed or relative organized files, the following additional functions can
        be applied: Use the START statement in sequential or dynamic access mode to alter
        the sequence of record retrieval; use the DELETE statement with any access mode to
        remove a record logically from a file; and use the WRITE statement in random or
        dynamic access mode to insert a new record into the file.

        LINAGE
        Use the LINAGE clause when specifying an output report. It facilitates definition of a
        logical page and the positioning within that logical page of top and bottom margins and
        a footing area. Use of the LINAGE clause implicitly defines an associated special
        register, the LINAGE-COUNTER that acts as a pointer to a line within the page body.

Exception Handling
        During the execution of any input or output operation, unusual conditions can arise
        that preclude normal completion of the operation. There are three methods by which
        these conditions are communicated to the object program: status keys, exception
        declaratives, and optional phrases associated with the imperative statement.

        IΓÇôO Status
        IΓÇôO status is a conceptual entity used in this document to facilitate exact specification
        of the status of the execution of an input-output operation. The setting of I-O status is
        affected only by the CLOSE, DELETE, OPEN, READ, REWRITE, START, and WRITE
        statements. The I-O status value for a given file is made available to the program
        through the data name specified in the FILE STATUS clause of the file control entry for
        that file. The I-O status value is placed into this data item during the execution of the
        input-output statement and prior to the execution of any imperative statement
        associated with that input-output statement or prior to the execution of any exception
        declarative.

        Exception Declaratives
        A USE AFTER EXCEPTION procedure, when one is specified for the file, is executed
        whenever an input or output condition arises that results in an unsuccessful
        input-output operation. However, the exception declarative is not executed if the
        condition is invalid key and the INVALID KEY phrase is specified or if the condition is at
        end and the AT END phrase is specified.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                 2ΓÇô3
Programming Considerations




        Optional Phrases
        The INVALID KEY phrase can be associated with the DELETE, READ, REWRITE, START,
        or WRITE statements. Some of the conditions that give rise to an invalid key condition
        are where:

        ΓÇó   A requested key does not exist in the file (DELETE, READ, or START statements).
        ΓÇó   A key is already in a file and duplicates are not allowed (WRITE statement).
        ΓÇó   A key does not exist in the file or when it was not the last key read (REWRITE
            statement).

        If the invalid key condition occurs during the execution of a statement for which the
        INVALID KEY phrase has been specified, the statement identified by that INVALID KEY
        phrase is executed.

        The AT END phrase can be associated with a READ statement. The atΓÇôend condition
        occurs in a sequentially accessed file when:

        ΓÇó   No next logical record exists in the file.
        ΓÇó   The number of significant digits in the relative record number is larger than the
            size of the relative key data item.
        ΓÇó   An optional file is not present.
        ΓÇó   READ statement is attempted and the atΓÇôend condition already exists.

        If the at-end condition occurs during the execution of a statement for which the AT
        END phrase has been specified, the statement identified by that AT END phrase is
        executed.

Rerun
        The rerun feature of COBOL provides a facility for checkpoint/restart. That is,
        executing a rerun takes a snapshot (checkpoint) of the program status and stores the
        information. It is then possible to restart the program from a rerun point. The RERUN
        clause protects the user from having to start a program over from the beginning if a
        hardware failure occurs while the job is running.

        There are two basic parts to the RERUN clause. You must designate a medium to
        receive the data and a criterion from which the frequency of checkpoints can be
        determined. The receiving medium can be specified by designating a separate
        hardware device. The determination of frequency of the dump is made on the basis of
        a number of records of a particular file having been processed.

                                                            Programming Considerations




2.3. Table Handling
        Tables of data are common components of business data processing problems.
        Although the repeating items that make up a table could be described otherwise by a
        series of separate data description entries all having the same level number and all
        subordinate to the same group item, there are two reasons why this approach is not
        satisfactory. First, from a documentation standpoint, the underlying homogeneity of
        the items would not be readily apparent. Second, the problem of making an individual
        element of such a table available would be severe when there is a decision as to
        which element is to be made available at object time.

        Tables of data items are defined in COBOL by including the OCCURS clause in their
        data description entries. This clause specifies that the item is to be repeated as many
        times as stated. The item is a table element, and its name and description apply to
        each repetition or occurrence. Since each occurrence of a table element does not
        have a unique data name assigned to it, reference to a desired occurrence can be
        made only by specifying the data name of the table element together with the
        occurrence number of the desired table element. The occurrence number is known as
        a subscript. The number of occurrences of a table element can be specified as fixed or
        variable.

2.3.1. Table Definition
        To define a one-dimensional table, you use an OCCURS clause as part of the data
        description of the table element, but the OCCURS clause must not appear in the
        description of group items that contains the table element. The following example
        shows a one-dimensional table defined by the item TABLE-ELEMENT.

        Example
           01    TABLE-1.
                02 TABLE-ELEMENT OCCURS 20 TIMES.
                    03    DOG . . .
                    03    FOX . . .

        Example
        In this example, TABLEΓÇôELEMENT defines a oneΓÇôdimensional table, but DOG does not
        since there is an OCCURS clause in the description of the group item (TABLE-
        ELEMENT) that contains DOG.

           02   TABLE-1.
                03 TABLE-ELEMENT OCCURS 20 TIMES.
                    04 DOG OCCURS 5 TIMES.
                         05 EASY . . .
                         05 FOX . . .

        In both examples, the complete set of occurrences of TABLE-ELEMENT has been
        assigned the name TABLE-1. However, it is not necessary to give a group name to the
        table unless it is desired to refer to the complete table as a group item.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                               2ΓÇô5
Programming Considerations




        None of the three one-dimensional tables that appear in the following two examples
        has a group name.

        Example
            01   ABLE.
                 02 BAKER . . .
                 02 CHARLIE OCCURS 20 TIMES . . .
                 02 DOG . . .

        Example
            01   ABLE.
                 02 BAKER OCCURS 20 TIMES . . .
                 02 CHARLIE . . .
                 02 DOG OCCURS 5 TIMES . . .

        Defining a one-dimensional table within each occurrence of an element of another
        one-dimensional table gives rise to a two-dimensional table. To define a two-
        dimensional table, an OCCURS clause must appear in the data description of the
        element of the table, and in the description of only one group item that contains that
        table element.

        Therefore, in the following example, DOG is an element of a two-dimensional table; it
        occurs five times within each element of the item BAKER, which itself occurs 20
        times. BAKER is an element of a one-dimensional table.

        Example
            02   BAKER OCCURS 20 TIMES . . .
                 03 CHARLIE . . .
                 03 DOG OCCURS 5 TIMES . . .

        In general, to define an nΓÇôdimensional table, the OCCURS clause must appear in the
        data description of the element of the table and in the descriptions of (nΓÇô1) group
        items that contain the element.

2.3.2. Initial Values of Tables
        In the working storage section, initial values of elements within tables are specified in
        one of the following ways:

        ΓÇó    The table can be described as a series of separate data description entries all
             subordinate to the same group item, each of which specifies the value of an
             element, or part of an element, of the table. In defining the record and its
             elements, any data description clause (USAGE, PICTURE, etc.) can be used to
             complete the definition, where required. The hierarchical structure of the table is
             then shown by use of the REDEFINES entry and its associated subordinate entries.
             The subordinate entries, following the REDEFINES entry, which is repeated due to
             OCCURS clauses, must not contain VALUE clauses.




2ΓÇô6                                                                               7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                              Programming Considerations




        ΓÇó   All the dimensions of a table can be initialized by associating the VALUE clause
            with the description of the entry defining the entire table. The lower-level entries
            show the hierarchical structure of the table; lower-level entries must not contain
            VALUE clauses.
        ΓÇó   The value of selected table elements can be specified using VALUE clauses.

2.3.3. Reference to Table Items
        Whenever you refer to a table element or a condition name associated with a table
        element, the reference must indicate which occurrence of the element is intended,
        except in a SEARCH statement. For access to a one-dimensional table, the occurrence
        number of the desired element provides complete information. For tables of more
        than one dimension, an occurrence number must be supplied for each dimension of
        the table accessed. In the last example of Section 2.3.1, a reference to the fourth
        BAKER or the fourth CHARLIE would be complete, whereas a reference to the fourth
        DOG would not be complete. For example, to refer to DOG, which is an element of a
        two-dimensional table, you must refer to the fourth DOG within the fifth BAKER.

2.3.4. Subscripting
        Occurrence numbers are specified by appending one or more subscripts to the data
        name.

        The subscript can be represented either by an integer, a data name that refers to an
        integer numeric elementary item, or an index name associated with the table. A data
        name or index name can be followed by either the operator + or the operator - and an
        integer, which is used as an increment or decrement, respectively. It is permissible to
        mix integers, data names, and index names.

        The subscripts, enclosed in parentheses are written immediately following any
        qualification for the name of the table element. The number of subscripts in such a
        reference must equal the number of dimensions in the table whose element is being
        referenced. That is, there must be a subscript for each OCCURS clause in the hierarchy
        containing the data name including the data name itself.

        When more than one subscript is required, they are written in order of successively
        less inclusive dimensions of the data organization. If a multidimensional table is
        thought of as a series of nested tables and the most inclusive or outermost table in
        the nest is considered to be the major table with the innermost or least inclusive table
        being the minor table, the subscripts are written from left to right in the order major,
        intermediate, and minor.

        A reference to an item must not be subscripted if the item is not a table element or an
        item or condition name within a table element.

        The lowest permissible occurrence number is 1. The highest permissible occurrence
        number in any particular case is the maximum number of occurrences of the item as
        specified in the OCCURS clause.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                 2ΓÇô7
Programming Considerations




Subscripting Using Integers or Data Names
        When an integer or data name is used to represent a subscript, it can be used to refer
        to items within different tables. These tables need not have elements of the same
        size. The same integer or data name can appear as the only subscript with one item
        and as one of two or more subscripts with another item.

Subscripting Using Index Names
        In order to facilitate such operations as table searching and manipulating specific
        items, a technique called indexing is available. To use this technique, you assign one or
        more index names to an item whose data description entry contains an OCCURS
        clause. An index associated with an index name acts as a subscript, and its value
        corresponds to an occurrence number for the item to which the index name is
        associated.

        The INDEXED BY phrase, by which the index name is identified and associated with its
        table, is an optional part of the OCCURS clause. There is no separate entry to describe
        the index associated with the index name since its definition is completely hardware
        oriented. At object time, the contents of the index correspond to an occurrence
        number for that specific dimension of the table with which the index is associated.

        When a reference is made to a table element, or to an item within a table element,
        and the name of the item is followed by its related index name or names in
        parentheses, then each occurrence number required to complete the reference is
        obtained from the respective index name. The index name acts as a subscript whose
        value is used in any table reference that specifies indexing.

        The initial value of an index at object time is undefined, and the index must be
        initialized before use. The initial value of an index is assigned using the PERFORM
        statement with the VARYING phrase, the SEARCH statement with the ALL phrase, or
        the SET statement.

        The use of an integer or data name as a subscript referencing a table element or an
        item within a table element does not cause the alteration of any index associated with
        that table.

        An index name can be used to reference only the table to which it is associated
        through the INDEXED BY phrase.

        Data that is arranged in the form of a table is often searched. The SEARCH statement
        provides facilities for producing serial and binary searches. It is used to search a table
        for a table element that satisfies a specific condition and to adjust the value of the
        associated index to indicate that table element.

        Relative indexing is an additional option for making references to a table element or to
        an item within a table element. When the name of a table element is followed by a
        subscript of the form (index name + or - integer), the occurrence number required to
        complete the reference is the same as if index name were set up or down by integer
        through the SET statement before the reference. The use of relative indexing does not
        cause the object program to alter the value of the index.



2ΓÇô8                                                                                7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                              Programming Considerations




        The value of an index can be made accessible to an object program by storing the
        value in an index data item. Index data items are described in the program by a data
        description entry containing a USAGE IS INDEX clause. The index value is moved to the
        index data item by the execution of a SET statement.

Subscripting Example
        Assume the following data definition:

           02   XCOUNTER . . .

           02   BAKER OCCURS 20 TIMES INDEXED BY BAKER-INDEX . . .
                03 CHARLIE . . .
                03 DOG OCCURS 5 TIMES . . .
                    04 EASY . . .
                    88 MAX VALUE IS . . .
                    04 FOX . . .
                        05 GEORGE OCCURS 10 TIMES . . .
                            06 HARRY . . .
                            06 JIM . . .

        References to BAKER and CHARLIE require only one subscript; references to DOG,
        EASY, MAX, and FOX require two; and references to GEORGE, HARRY, and JIM require
        three.

        To illustrate the requirement of order from major to minor, HARRY (18, 2, 7) means the
        HARRY in the seventh GEORGE, in the second DOG, in the eighteenth BAKER.

        Mixing arithmetic expressions and index names is illustrated by HARRY
        (BAKER-INDEX, 4, XCOUNTER + 5).


2.4. Language Concepts
        The language considerations and rules specified in this section apply to the highest
        level of UCS COBOL. When a particular level of a module does not allow all of these
        language concepts, the restrictions is pointed out in the section describing that
        language element. Note that restrictions contained in one module might affect other
        modules. For example, qualification is not allowed in level 1 of the Nucleus; therefore,
        any module that is combined with level 1 of the Nucleus would have the same
        restriction.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                2ΓÇô9
Programming Considerations




2.4.1. Notation Used in General Formats
        A general format is the specific arrangement of the elements of a clause or a
        statement. A clause or a statement consists of elements as defined in the following
        subsections. Throughout this manual, a format is shown adjacent to information
        defining the clause or statement. When more than one specific arrangement is
        permitted, the general format is separated into numbered formats. Clauses must be
        written in the sequence given in the general formats. (Clauses that are optional must
        appear in the sequence shown if they are used.) In certain cases, stated explicitly in
        the rules associated with a given format, the clauses can appear in sequences other
        than that shown. Applications, requirements, or restrictions are shown as rules (see
        Section 2.4.2).

Elements
        The elements that make up a clause or a statement consist of uppercase words,
        lowercase words, level numbers, brackets, braces, connectives, and special
        characters.

Words
        All underlined uppercase words are called keywords and are required when the
        functions of which they are a part are used. Uppercase words that are not underlined
        are optional to the user and need not be written in the source program. Uppercase
        words, whether underlined or not, must be spelled correctly.

        Lowercase words (in italics), in a general format, are generic terms used to represent
        UCS COBOL words, literals, PICTURE character strings, comment entries, or a
        complete syntactical entry that must be supplied by the user. Where generic terms
        are repeated in a general format, a number appendage to the term serves to identify
        that term for explanation or discussion.

Level Numbers
        When specific level numbers appear in data description entry formats, those specific
        level numbers are required when such entries are used in an UCS COBOL program. In
        this manual, the form 01, 02, . . . , 09 is used to indicate level numbers 1 through 9.

Brackets, Braces, and Choice Indicators
        When brackets, [ ], enclose a portion of a general format, one of the options contained
        within the brackets can be explicitly specified or that portion of the general format can
        be omitted.

        When braces, { }, enclose a portion of a general format, one of the options contained
        within the braces must be either explicitly specified or implicitly selected. If one of the
        options contains only reserved words that are not keywords, then that option is the
        default option. This option is implicitly selected unless one of the options is explicitly
        specified.




2ΓÇô10                                                                               7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                  Programming Considerations




        When choice indicators {| |} enclose a portion of a general format, one or more of the
        unique options contained within the choice indicators must be specified, but a single
        option can be specified only once.

        Options are indicated in a general format or a portion of a general format by vertically
        stacking alternative possibilities, by a series of brackets, braces, or choice indicators
        or by a combination of both. An option is selected by specifying one of the
        possibilities from a stack of alternative possibilities or by specifying a unique
        combination of possibilities from a series of brackets, braces, or choice indicators.

The Ellipsis
        In text, other than general formats, the ellipsis ( ... ) shows the omission of a word or
        words when such omission does not impair comprehension.

        In general formats, the ellipsis represents the position at which the user elects
        repetition of a portion of a format. The portion of the format that can be repeated is
        determined as follows:

        Given an ellipsis ( ... ) in a clause or statement format, find the right bracket (]) or right
        brace (}) immediately to the left of the ellipsis. Find the logically matching left bracket
        ([) or left brace ({). The ellipsis applies to the words between the pair of delimiters.

Format Punctuation
        The separators comma and semicolon can be used anywhere the separator space is
        used in the formats (see Section 2.4.5). In the source program, these separators are
        interchangeable. The separator period, when used in the formats, has the status of a
        required word.

Use of Special Character Words in Formats
        The special character words +, -, >, <, =, <=, and >=, when appearing in formats,
        although not underlined, are required when such portions of the formats are used.

2.4.2. Rules
        This subsection describes syntax rules and general rules you must follow when
        programming in COBOL.

        Syntax Rules
        Syntax rules define or clarify the order in which words or elements are arranged to
        form larger elements such as phrases, clauses, or statements. Syntax rules also either
        can impose restrictions on individual words or elements or can relax restrictions
        implied by words or elements.

        These rules are used to define or clarify how the statement must be written; that is,
        the order of the elements of the statement and restrictions or amplifications of what
        each element can represent.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                      2ΓÇô11
Programming Considerations




        General Rules
        A general rule defines or clarifies the meaning or relationship of meanings of an
        element or set of elements. It is used to define or clarify the semantics of the
        statement and the effect that it has on either execution or compilation.

2.4.3. Character Set
        The most basic and indivisible unit of the language is the character. The set of
        characters used to form UCS COBOL character strings and separators includes the
        letters of the alphabet, digits, and special characters. The character set consists of the
        characters as defined under COBOL character set in the Glossary. In the case of
        nonnumeric literals, comment entries, and comment lines, the character set is
        expanded to include the computer's entire character set. The characters allowable in
        each type of character string and as separators are defined in Section 2.4.5.

2.4.4. Language Structure
        The individual characters of the language are concatenated to form character strings
        and separators. A separator can be concatenated with another separator or with a
        character string. A character string can only be concatenated with a separator. The
        concatenation of character strings and separators forms the text of a source program.

2.4.5. Separators
        A separator is a character or two contiguous characters formed according to the
        following rules:

        ΓÇó   The punctuation character space is a separator. Anywhere a space is used as a
            separator or part of a separator, more than one space can be used. All spaces
            immediately following the separators comma, semicolon, and period are
            considered part of that separator and are not considered to be the separator
            space.
        ΓÇó   Except when the comma is used in a PICTURE character string, the punctuation
            characters comma and semicolon, immediately followed by a space, are
            separators that can be used anywhere the separator space is used. They can be
            used to improve program readability.
        ΓÇó   The punctuation character period, when followed by a space, is a separator. It
            must be used to indicate the end of a sentence, or as shown in formats.
        ΓÇó   The punctuation characters right and left parentheses are separators. Parentheses
            can appear only in balanced pairs of left and right parentheses delimiting
            subscripts, reference modifiers, function arguments, arithmetic expressions, or
            conditions.
        ΓÇó   The punctuation character quotation mark is a separator. An opening quotation
            mark must be immediately preceded by a space or left parenthesis; a closing
            quotation mark, when paired with an opening quotation mark, must be
            immediately followed by one of the separators space, comma, semicolon, period,
            or right parenthesis.




2ΓÇô12                                                                              7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                             Programming Considerations




        ΓÇó   Pseudotext delimiters are separators. An opening pseudotext delimiter must be
            immediately preceded by a space; a closing pseudotext delimiter must be
            immediately followed by one of the separators space, comma, semicolon, or
            period. Pseudotext delimiters can appear only in balanced pairs delimiting pseudoΓÇô
            text.
        ΓÇó   The punctuation character colon is a separator and is required when shown in the
            general formats.
        ΓÇó   The separator space can immediately precede all separators except:
            ΓêÆ   As specified by reference format rules (see Section 2.4.6).
            ΓêÆ   The separator closing quotation mark. In this case, a preceding space is
                considered as part of the nonnumeric literal and not as a separator. The
                opening pseudoΓÇôtext delimiter, where the preceding space is required.
        ΓÇó   The separator space can immediately follow any separator except the opening
            quotation mark. In this case, a following space is considered as part of the
            nonnumeric literal and not as a separator.

        Any punctuation character that appears as part of the specification of a PICTURE
        character string or numeric literal is not considered as a punctuation character, but
        rather as a symbol used in the specification of that PICTURE character string or
        numeric literal. PICTURE character strings are delimited only by the separators space,
        comma, semicolon, or period.

        The rules established for the formation of separators do not apply to the characters
        that comprise the contents of nonnumeric literals, comment entries, or comment
        lines.

2.4.6. Character Strings
        A character string is a character or a sequence of contiguous characters that forms a
        COBOL word, a literal, a PICTURE character string, or a comment entry. A character
        string is delimited by separators.

2.4.7. COBOL Words
        A COBOL word is a character string of not more than 30 characters that form a
        user-defined word, a system name, a reserved word, or a function name. Each
        character of a COBOL word is selected from the set of letters, digits, and the hyphen.
        The hyphen cannot appear as the first or last character. Each lowercase letter is
        considered equivalent to its corresponding uppercase letter. Within a source program,
        reserved words and user-defined words form disjoint sets; reserved words and
        system names form disjoint sets; reserved words and function names form disjoint
        sets; function names, system names, and user-defined words form intersecting sets.

        The same COBOL word can be used as a function name, as a system name, and as a
        user-defined word within a source program. The class of a specific occurrence of this
        COBOL word is determined by the context of the clause or phrase in which it occurs.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                              2ΓÇô13
Programming Considerations




User-Defined Words
        A user-defined word is a COBOL word that the user must supply to satisfy the format
        of a clause or statement. Each character of a user-defined word is selected from the
        set of characters A through Z, 0 through 9, and ΓÇô, except that - cannot appear as the
        first or last character.

        The types of user-defined words are:

        ΓÇó   Alphabet name
        ΓÇó   Class name
        ΓÇó   Condition name
        ΓÇó   Data name
        ΓÇó   File name
        ΓÇó   Index name
        ΓÇó   Level number
        ΓÇó   Library name
        ΓÇó   Mnemonic name
        ΓÇó   Paragraph name
        ΓÇó   Program name
        ΓÇó   Record name
        ΓÇó   Report name
        ΓÇó   Routine name
        ΓÇó   Section name
        ΓÇó   Segment number
        ΓÇó   Symbolic character
        ΓÇó   Text name

        Within a given source program, but not in any contained program, the user-defined
        words are grouped into the following disjoint sets:

        ΓÇó   Alphabet names
        ΓÇó   Class names
        ΓÇó   Condition names, data names, and record names
        ΓÇó   File names
        ΓÇó   Index names
        ΓÇó   Library names
        ΓÇó   Mnemonic names
        ΓÇó   Paragraph names

        ΓÇó   Program names
        ΓÇó   Report names
        ΓÇó   Routine names
        ΓÇó   Section names
        ΓÇó   Symbolic characters
        ΓÇó   Text names

        All user-defined words, except segment numbers and level numbers, can belong to
        only one of these disjoint sets. Further, all user-defined words within a given disjoint
        set must be unique, except as specified in the rules for uniqueness of reference. (See
        Section 2.4.20.)

        With the exception of section names, paragraph names, segment numbers, and level
        numbers, all user-defined words must contain at least one alphabetic character. Level
        numbers and segment numbers need not be unique. A given specification of a level
        number or segment number can be identical to any other level number.

        ΓÇó   Condition names
            A condition name is a name assigned to a specific value, set of values, or range of
            values, within a complete set of values that a data item can assume. The data item
            itself is called a conditional variable.
            Condition names can be defined in the Data Division or in the SPECIAL-NAMES
            paragraph of the Environment Division where a condition name must be assigned
            to the on status or off status, or both, of implementor-defined switches.
            A condition name is used in conditions as an abbreviation for the relation
            condition. This relation condition defines the associated conditional variable as
            equal to one of the set of values to which that condition name is assigned. A
            condition name is also used in a SET statement, indicating that the associated
            value is to be moved to the conditional variable.
        ΓÇó   Mnemonic name
            A mnemonic name assigns a user-defined word to an implementor name. These
            associations are established in the SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph of the Environment
            Division. (See Section 3.4.5.)
        ΓÇó   Paragraph name
            A paragraph name is a word that names a paragraph in the Procedure Division.
            Paragraph names are equivalent only if they are composed of the same sequence
            of the same number of digits and characters.
        ΓÇó   Section name
            A section name is a word that names a section in the Procedure Division. Section
            names are equivalent only if they are composed of the same sequence of the
            same number of digits and characters.
        ΓÇó   Other user-defined names
            See the Glossary for definitions of all other types of user-defined words.

Programming Considerations




System Names
        A system name is a COBOL word that is used to communicate with the operating
        environment. Each character used in the formation of a system name must be
        selected from the set of characters A through Z, 0 through 9, and minus (-), except
        that - cannot appear as the first or last character.

        There are three types of system names:

        ΓÇó   Computer names
        ΓÇó   Implementor names
        ΓÇó   Language names

        These three types of system names form disjoint sets. A given system name can
        belong to one and only one of them.

        Computer name and implementor name are individually defined in the Glossary.

Reserved Words
        A reserved word is a COBOL word from a specified list of words that can be used in
        COBOL source programs, but which must not appear in the programs as user-defined
        words or system names. Reserved words can be used only as specified in the general
        formats. (See Appendix A.)

        ΓÇó   Reserved words satisfy the following conditions:
        ΓÇó   Reserved words do not begin with the characters 0 through 9, X, Y, or Z, except
            for the reserved words ZERO, ZEROES, and ZEROS.
        ΓÇó   Reserved words do not contain only one alphabetic character.
        ΓÇó   Reserved words do not start with one or two characters followed by "-" except for
            the reserved words I-O, I-O-CONTROL, and reserved words that begin with 'B-' or
            'DB-'.
        ΓÇó   Reserved words do not contain two or more contiguous hyphens.

        There are three types of reserved words:

        ΓÇó   Required words
        ΓÇó   Optional words
        ΓÇó   Special-purpose words




2ΓÇô16                                                                            7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                              Programming Considerations




Required Words
        A required word is a word whose presence is required when the format in which the
        word appears is used in a source program.

        Required words are of two types:

        ΓÇó   Keywords. Within each format, such words are uppercase and underlined.
        ΓÇó   Special-character words. These are the arithmetic operators and relation
            characters.

Optional Words
        Within each format, uppercase words that are not underlined are called optional
        words and can be specified at the userΓÇÖs option with no effect on the semantics of the
        format.

SpecialΓÇôPurpose Words
        There are two types of special-purpose words:

        ΓÇó   Special registers
            Certain reserved words are used to name and refer to special registers. Special
            registers are certain compiler-generated storage areas primarily used to store
            information produced in conjunction with the use of specific COBOL features.
            Unless noted otherwise in these specifications, one special register of each type
            is allocated for each program. In the general formats of this specification, a special
            register can be used, unless otherwise restricted, wherever data name or
            identifier is specified, provided that the special register is the same category as
            the data name or identifier. If qualification is allowed, special registers can be
            qualified as necessary to provide uniqueness. (See Section 2.4.20)
            There are three special registers:
            ΓêÆ   LINAGE-COUNTER (see Section 4.2.8)
            ΓêÆ   LINE-COUNTER (see Section 10.1.5)
            ΓêÆ   PAGE-COUNTER (see Section 10.1.4)
        ΓÇó   Figurative constants
            Certain reserved words are used to name and refer to specific constant values.
            These reserved words are specified in Section 2.4.8.

Function Names
        A function name is a word that is one of a specified list of words that can be used in
        COBOL source programs. The same word, in a different context, can appear in a
        program as a user-defined word or a system name. (See Section 2.4.20).

2.4.8. Literals
        A literal is a character string whose value is implied by an ordered set of characters, of
        which the literal is composed, or by specification of a reserved word that refers to a
        figurative constant. Every literal belongs to one of two types: nonnumeric or numeric.

Nonnumeric Literals
        A nonnumeric literal is a character string delimited on both ends by the separator
        quotation mark or the separator apostrophe. The nonnumeric literal must be delimited
        on each end by the same character. The length of a nonnumeric literal applies to its
        representation in the object program.

        A nonnumeric literal can be 1 through 160 characters in length.

        General Format
             "{character-1}... "

        Syntax Rules
        1.    Character-1 can be any character in the computer character set.
        2.    If character-1 is to represent the quotation mark, and the literal is delimited by
              quotation marks, two contiguous quotation mark characters must be used to
              represent a single occurrence of that character.
        3.    If character-1 is to represent an apostrophe, and the literal is delimited by an
              apostrophe, two contiguous apostrophe characters must be used to represent a
              single occurrence of that character.

        General Rules
        1.    The value of a nonnumeric literal in the object program is the value represented by
              character-1.
        2.    The separator quotation mark or apostrophe that delimits the nonnumeric literal is
              not part of the value of the nonnumeric literal.
        3.    All nonnumeric literals are of category alphanumeric.




2ΓÇô18                                                                                 7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                  Programming Considerations




Numeric Literals
        There are two types of numeric literals: fixed-point and floating-point.

        FixedΓÇôpoint literal
        A fixedΓÇôpoint literal is a character string whose characters are selected from the digits
        0 through 9, the plus sign, the minus sign, and the decimal point. Fixed-point literals of
        1 through 18 digits in length are allowed. The rules for the formation of fixed-point
        literals are:

        ΓÇó    A literal must contain at least one digit.
        ΓÇó    A literal must not contain more than one sign character. If a sign is used, it must
             appear as the leftmost character of the literal. If the literal is unsigned, the literal is
             nonnegative.
        ΓÇó    A literal must not contain more than one decimal point. The decimal point is
             treated as an assumed decimal point and can appear anywhere within the literal
             except as the rightmost character. If the literal contains no decimal point, the
             literal is an integer.
             If a literal conforms to the rules for the formation of numeric literals but is
             enclosed in quotation marks, it is a nonnumeric literal and is treated as such by the
             compiler.
        ΓÇó    The value of a numeric literal is the algebraic quantity represented by the
             characters in the numeric literal. Every numeric literal is category numeric. (See
             Section 3.5.11.) The size of a numeric literal in standard data format characters is
             equal to the number of digits specified by the user.

        FloatingΓÇôpoint literal
        A floating-point literal is a character string whose characters are selected from the
        numerals 0 through 9, the plus sign, the minus sign, the decimal point, and the
        character E.

        A floating-point literal must have the following format:

            [┬▒] mantissa E [┬▒] exponent

        where

             ┬▒

                 are the plus or minus signs (optional).

             mantissa

                 consists of 1 to 18 digits with a required decimal point; the decimal point can
                 appear in any position. If the mantissa is signed, the sign must be the leftmost
                 character in the literal string. If the mantissa is unsigned, the literal value is
                 positive.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                      2ΓÇô19
Programming Considerations




              E

                  must immediately follow the mantissa, and the exponent must appear
                  immediately to the right of the character E.

              exponent

                  consists of one to three digits and an optional sign. If the sign is present, it
                  must be immediately to the right of the character E and immediately to the left
                  of the digits. Unsigned exponents are positive. The exponent cannot contain a
                  decimal point.

        The largest number that can be represented by a floating-point literal for double
        precision is 0.89884656743115795 X 10 308 and the smallest that can be represented is

        0.27813423231340018 x 10 -308 . For single precision, the largest number is 0.17014118
        x10 39 and the smallest number is 0.14693680 x 10 -38.

        The value of a floating-point literal is the algebraic quantity product of the mantissa
        and 10 raised to the power given by the exponent.

        Example
             +1.5E-2 = 1.5 x 10-2

Figurative Constant Values
        Figurative constant values are generated by the compiler and are referred to through
        the use of the reserved words that follow. These words must not be bounded by
        quotation marks when used as figurative constants. The singular and plural forms of
        figurative constants are equivalent and can be used interchangeably.

        The figurative constant values and the reserved words used to refer to them are

        1.    [ALL] ZERO, [ALL] ZEROS, [ALL] ZEROES
              Represent the numeric value 0, or one or more of the character 0 from the
              computer's character set.
        2.    [ALL] SPACE, [ALL] SPACES
              Represent one or more of the character spaces from the computerΓÇÖs character
              set.
        3.    [ALL] HIGHΓÇôVALUE, [ALL] HIGHΓÇôVALUES
              Except in the SPECIALΓÇôNAMES paragraph, represent one or more of the
              characters that have the highest ordinal position in the program collating
              sequence.
        4. [ALL] LOWΓÇôVALUE, [ALL] LOWΓÇôVALUES
              Except in the SPECIALΓÇôNAMES paragraph, represent one or more of the
              characters that have the lowest ordinal position in the program collating sequence.

        5.   [ALL] QUOTE, [ALL] QUOTES
             Represent one or more of the character quotation mark (") or apostrophe (ΓÇÖ),
             depending upon the keyword option used. (See Table 4.2.) The word QUOTE or
             QUOTES cannot be used in place of a quotation mark in a source program to bind
             a nonnumeric literal. Therefore, QUOTE ABD QUOTE is incorrect as a way of
             stating the nonnumeric literal ΓÇ£ABDΓÇ¥.
        6. ALL literal
             Represents all or part of the string generated by successive concatenations of the
             characters comprising the literal. The literal must be a nonnumeric literal. The
             literal must not be a figurative constant.
        7.   [ALL] symbolic-character
             Represents one or more of the character specified as the value of this symbolic
             character in the SYMBOLIC CHARACTERS clause of the SPECIALΓÇôNAMES
             paragraph (see Section 3.4.5).

             Represents the value used to indicate that the data items defined with USAGE
             POINTER or the ADDRESS OF phrase do not contain a valid address. NULL can be

        When a figurative constant represents a string of one or more characters, the length
        of the string is determined by the compiler from context according to the following
        rules:

        1.   When a figurative constant is specified in a VALUE clause or when a figurative
             constant is associated with another data item, as when the figurative constant is
             moved to or compared with another data item, the string of characters specified
             by the figurative constant is repeated character by character on the right until the
             size of the resultant string is greater than or equal to the number of character
             positions in the associated data item. The resultant string is then truncated from
             the right until it is equal to the number of character positions in the associated
             data item. This is done prior to, and independent of, the application of any
             JUSTIFIED clause that can be associated with the data item.
        2.   When a figurative constant, other than ALL literal, is not associated with another
             data item, as when the figurative constant appears in a DISPLAY, STOP, STRING,
             or UNSTRING statement, the length of the string is one character.
        3.   When the figurative constant ALL literal is not associated with another data item,
             the length of the string is the length of the literal.
