Nucleus




             if 1000, 100, 1, 0, and .01, respectively, are moved to the edited field.
             To avoid truncation, the minimum size of the PICTURE character string for the
             receiving data item must be the number of characters in the sending data item,
             plus the number of nonfloating insertion characters being edited into the receiving
             data item, plus one for the floating insertion character. If truncation does occur,
             the value of the data that is used for editing is the value after truncation (see
             Section 2.4.19).
             In a given PICTURE character string, floating insertion and fixed insertion of the
             same symbol are disallowed. Also illegal is the specification of more than one type
             of floating insertion editing, or a mixture of floating insertion and suppression and
             replacement editing. In addition, a PICTURE character string can contain only one
             type of sign control editing or none.
          9. Zero suppression editing
             The suppression of leading zeros in numeric character positions is indicated by the
             use of the alphabetic character Z or the asterisk (*) as suppression symbols in a
             PICTURE character string. These symbols are mutually exclusive in a given
             PICTURE character string. Each suppression symbol is counted in determining the
             size of the item. If Z is used, the replacement character is the space and if the
             asterisk is used, the replacement character is *.
             Zero suppression and replacement are indicated in a PICTURE character string by
             using a string of one or more of the allowable symbols to represent leading
             numeric character positions that are to be replaced when the associated character
             position in the data contains a leading zero. Any of the simple insertion characters
             embedded in the string of symbols or to the immediate right of this string is part
             of the string.
             In a PICTURE character string, there are only two ways of representing zero
             suppression. One way is to represent any or all of the leading numeric character
             positions to the left of the decimal point by suppression symbols. The other way
             is to represent all of the numeric character positions in the PICTURE character
             string by suppression symbols.
             If the suppression symbols appear only to the left of the decimal point, any leading
             zero in the data that corresponds to a symbol in the string is replaced by the
             replacement character. Suppression terminates at the first nonzero digit in the
             data represented by the suppression symbol string or at the decimal point,
             whichever is encountered first.
             If all numeric character positions in the PICTURE character string are represented
             by suppression symbols and the value of the data is not zero, the result is the
             same as if the suppression characters were only to the left of the decimal point. If
             the value is zero and the suppression symbol is Z, the entire data item, including
             any editing characters, is spaces. If the value is zero and the suppression symbol
             is *, the data item, including any insertion editing symbols except the actual
             decimal point, is *. In this case, the actual decimal point will appear in the data
             item.
          10. The symbols +, - , *, Z, and the currency symbol, when used as floating
              replacement characters, are mutually exclusive within a given character string.

Precedence Rules
        Figure 3ΓÇô1 shows the order of precedence for symbols in a PICTURE character string.
        An X at an intersection indicates that the symbols at the top of the column can
        precede (but not necessarily immediately) the symbols at the left of the row in a given
        character string. Arguments appearing in braces ({ }) indicate that the symbols are
        mutually exclusive. The currency symbol is indicated by the symbol cs.

        At least one of the symbols A, X, Z, 1, 9, or *, or at least two occurrences of one of the
        symbols +, - , or cs must be present in a PICTURE character string.

        Nonfloating insertion symbols + and - , floating insertion symbols Z, *, +, - , and cs, and
        other symbol P appear twice in Figure 3ΓÇô1. The leftmost column and uppermost row
        for each symbol represent its use to the left of the decimal point position. The second
        appearance of the symbol in the chart represents its use to the right of the decimal
        point position.

3.5.12. The REDEFINES Clause
          Function
          The REDEFINES clause allows the same computer storage area to be described by
          different data description entries.

          General Format




          Note: Level-number, data-name-1, and FILLER are shown in this format to improve
          clarity. Level-number, data-name-1, and FILLER are not part of the REDEFINES
          clause.




3ΓÇô40                                                                                       7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                                          Nucleus




        Syntax Rules
        1.   The REDEFINES clause, when specified, must immediately follow the subject of
             the entry.
        2.   The level numbers of data-name-2 and the subject of the entry must be identical,
             but must not be 66 or 88.
        3.   This clause must not be used in level 01 entries in the File Section.
        4. The data description entry for data-name-2 cannot contain an OCCURS clause.
           However, data-name-2 can be subordinate to an item whose data description
           entry contains an OCCURS clause. In this case, the reference to data-name-2 in
           the REDEFINES clause cannot be subscripted. Neither the original definition nor the
           redefinition can include a variable occurrence data item.
        5.   If the data item referred to by data-name-2 is either declared to be an external
             data record or is specified with a level number other than 01, the number of
             character positions it contains must be greater than or equal to the number of
             character positions in the data item referred to by the subject of this entry. If the
             data name referred to by data-name-2 is specified with a level number of 01 and is
             not declared to be an external data record, there is no such constraint.
        6. Data-name-2 must not be qualified even if it is not unique since no ambiguity of
           reference exists in this case because of the required placement of the REDEFINES
           clause within the source program.
        7.   Multiple redefinitions of the same character or bit positions are permitted. Multiple
             redefinitions of the same character or bit positions must all use the data name of
             the entry that originally defined the area.
        8. The entries giving the new description of the character positions must not contain
           any VALUE clauses, except in condition name entries.
        9. No entry having a level number numerically lower than the level number of
           data-name-2 and the subject of the entry can occur between the data description
           entries of data-name-2 and the subject of the entry.
        10. The entries giving the new descriptions of the character or bit positions must
            follow the entries defining the area of data-name-2, without intervening entries
            that define new character or bit positions.
        11. In level 1, data-name-2 cannot be subordinate to any entry that contains a
            REDEFINES clause. In level 2, data-name-2 can be subordinate to an entry that
            contains a REDEFINES clause.

        General Rules
        1.   Storage allocation starts at data-name-2 and continues over a storage area
             sufficient to contain the area of character or bit positions in the data item referred
             to by the data-name-1 or FILLER clause.
        2.   When the same character or bit position is defined by more than one data
             description entry, the data name associated with any of those data description
             entries can be used to refer to that character or bit position.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                  3ΓÇô41
Nucleus




3.5.13. The RENAMES Clause
          Function
          The RENAMES clause permits alternative, possibly overlapping, groupings of
          elementary items.

          General Format




          Note: The level-number "66" and data-name-1 are shown in this format to improve
          clarity. The level number and data-name-1 are not part of the RENAMES clause.

          Syntax Rules
          1.   Any number of RENAMES entries can be written for a logical record.
               All RENAMES entries referring to data items within a given logical record must
               immediately follow the last data description entry of the associated record
               description entry.
          2.   Data-name-1 cannot be used as a qualifier, and can only be qualified by the names
               of the associated level 01, FD, or SD entries. Neither data-name-2 nor data-name-3
               can have an OCCURS clause in its data description entry nor can be subordinate to
               an item that has an OCCURS clause in its data description entry.
          3.   Data-name-2 and data-name-3 must be names of elementary items or groups of
               elementary items in the same logical record, and cannot be the same data name. A
               66 level entry cannot rename another 66 level entry nor can it rename a 77, 88, or
               01 level entry.
          4. Data-name-2 and data-name-3 can be qualified.
          5.   None of the items within the range, including data-name-2 and data-name-3, if
               specified, can be variable occurrence data items.
          6. The words THROUGH and THRU are equivalent.
          7.   The beginning of the area described by data-name-3 must not be to the left of the
               beginning of the area described by data-name-2. The end of the area described by
               data-name-3 must be to the right of the end of the area described by data-name-2.
               Data-name-3, therefore, cannot be subordinate to data-name-2.

          The RENAMES entry can, however, span an entire table or array. If it does, the size of
          the RENAMES item includes any unused main storage introduced by elementary or
          group item synchronization.




3ΓÇô42                                                                              7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                                        Nucleus




        For example the following sequence is legal:

              02 B
                 03 C OCCURS 3 TIMES
                 03 D OCCURS 3 TIMES
                    04 E
                    04 F
                 03 G
              02 H
              66 J RENAMES B THRU H

        However, the following sequence alone is not correct.

             66 K RENAMES C THRU F

        The following sequence results in K being the first six characters in either A or B, and
        L being the third through seventh character in either A or B.

             02 A.
                03 D PIC X(2).
                03 C PIC X(2).
                03 G
                   04 E PIC X(2).
                   04 F PIC X(2).
             02 B REDEFINES A.
                03 H PIC X(3).
                03 I PIC X(4).
                03 J PIC X.
              66 K RENAMES D THRU E.
              66 L RENAMES C THRU I.

        General Rules
        1.    When data-name-3 is specified, data-name-1 is a group item that includes all
              elementary items starting with data-name-2 (if data-name-2 is an elementary item)
              or the first elementary item in data-name-2 (if data-name-2 is a group item), and
              concluding with data-name-3 (if data-name-3 is an elementary item) or the last
              elementary item in data-name-3 (if data-name-3 is a group item).
        2.    When data-name-3 is not specified, all of the data attributes of data-name-2
              become the data attributes for data-name-1.
        3.    The usage, and therefore the initial alignment, of a RENAMES entry is determined
              by the usage of the data-name-2 or the first elementary item in data-name-2 (if
              data-name-2 is a group item).
              An elementary data item, or an elementary data item subordinate to a group item
              whose declaration contains a USAGE specifying BINARY-1, must be declared with
              a PICTURE character string that describes an exact binary data item, that is, a
              PICTURE character string that contains only the symbols S and 1 (see Section
              3.5.11).

3.5.14. The SIGN Clause
          Function
          The SIGN clause specifies the position and the mode of representation of the
          operational sign when it is necessary to describe these properties explicitly.

          General Format




          Syntax Rules
          1.   The SIGN clause can be specified only for a numeric data description entry whose
               PICTURE contains the character S, or a group item containing at least one such
               numeric data description entry.
          2.   The numeric data description entries to which the SIGN clause applies must be
               described, implicitly or explicitly, as USAGE IS DISPLAY.
          3.   If the CODE-SET clause is specified in a file description entry, any signed numeric
               data description entries associated with that file description entry must be
               described with the SIGN IS SEPARATE clause.

          General Rules
          1.   The optional SIGN clause, if present, specifies the position and the mode of
               representation of the operational sign for the numeric data description entry to
               which it applies, or for each numeric data description entry subordinate to the
               group to which it applies. The SIGN clause applies only to numeric data description
               entries whose PICTURE contains the character S; the S indicates the presence, but
               neither the representation nor, necessarily, the position, of the operational sign.
          2.   If a SIGN clause is specified in a group item subordinate to a group item for which
               a SIGN clause is specified, the SIGN clause specified in the subordinate group item
               takes precedence for that subordinate group item.
          3.   If a SIGN clause is specified in an elementary numeric data description entry
               subordinate to a group item for which a SIGN clause is specified, the SIGN clause
               specified in the subordinate elementary numeric data description entry takes
               precedence for that elementary numeric data item.
          4. A numeric data description entry whose PICTURE contains the character S, but to
             which no optional SIGN clause applies, has an operational sign, but neither the
             representation nor, necessarily, the position of the operational sign is specified by
             the character S. In this (default) case, the operational sign is represented as an
             overpunch character (see Table 3ΓÇô1). General rules 5 through 7 do not apply to
             such signed numeric data items.




3ΓÇô44                                                                                7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                                          Nucleus




        5.   If the optional SEPARATE CHARACTER phrase is not present
             a.   The operational sign is presumed to be associated with the leading (or,
                  respectively, trailing) digit position of the elementary numeric data item.
             b. The letter S in a PICTURE character string is not counted in determining the
                size of the item (in terms of standard data format characters).
             c.   The valid signs for data items are listed in Table 3ΓÇô1.
        6. If the optional SEPARATE CHARACTER phrase is present
             a.   The operational sign is presumed to be the leading (or, respectively, trailing)
                  character position of the elementary numeric data item. This character position
                  is not a digit position.
             b. The letter S in a PICTURE character string is counted in determining the size of
                the item (in terms of standard data format characters).
             c.   The operational signs for positive and negative are the standard data format
                  characters + and -, respectively.
        7.   Every numeric data description entry whose PICTURE contains the character S is a
             signed numeric data description entry. If a SIGN clause applies to such an entry
             and conversion is necessary for purposes of computation or comparisons,
             conversion takes place automatically.

3.5.15. The SYNCHRONIZED Clause
        Function
        The SYNCHRONIZED clause specifies the alignment of an elementary item on the
        natural boundaries of the computer storage.

        General Format




        Syntax Rules
        1.   This clause can appear only with an elementary item.
        2.   SYNC is an abbreviation for SYNCHRONIZED.

        General Rules
        1.   This clause specifies that the subject data item is to be aligned in the computer
             such that no other data item occupies any of the bit positions between the
             leftmost and rightmost natural boundaries delimiting this data item. If the number
             of bit positions required to store this data item is less than the number of bit
             positions between those natural boundaries, the unused bits must not be used for
             any other data item. Such unused bits, however, are included in:
             a.   The size of any group items to which the elementary item belongs.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                   3ΓÇô45
Nucleus




               b. The number of bits allocated when any such group item is the object of a
                  REDEFINES clause. The unused bits are not included in the bits redefined when
                  the elementary item is the object of a REDEFINES clause.
          2.   SYNCHRONIZED followed by neither RIGHT nor LEFT specifies that the elementary
               item is to be SYNCHRONIZED LEFT if alphanumeric and SYNCHRONIZED RIGHT if
               numeric.
          3.   SYNCHRONIZED LEFT specifies that the elementary item is to be positioned such
               that it begins at the left character position of the natural boundary in which the
               elementary item is placed.
          4. SYNCHRONIZED RIGHT specifies that the elementary item is to be positioned such
             that it terminates on the right character position of the natural boundary in which
             the elementary item is placed.
          5.   Whenever a SYNCHRONIZED item is referred to in the source program, the
               original size of the item, as shown in the PICTURE clause, the USAGE clause, and
               the SIGN clause, is used in determining any action that depends on size, such as
               justification, truncation, or overflow.
          6. If the data description of an item contains an operational sign and any form of the
             SYNCHRONIZED clause, the sign of the item appears in the sign position explicitly
             or implicitly specified by the SIGN clause.
          7.   When the SYNCHRONIZED clause is specified in a data description entry of a data
               item that also contains an OCCURS clause, or in a data description entry of a data
               item subordinate to a data description entry that contains an OCCURS clause
               a.   Each occurrence of the data item is SYNCHRONIZED.
               b. Any implicit FILLER generated for other data items within that same table are
                  generated for each occurrence of those data items. (See general rule 8b.)
          8. This clause is hardware-dependent and, in addition to rules 1 through 7, the
             elementary items associated with this clause are handled as follows:
               a.   The format on the external media of records or groups containing elementary
                    items whose data description contains the SYNCHRONIZED clause is the same
                    as the internal format.
               b. Any necessary generation of implicit FILLER, if the elementary item
                  immediately preceding an item containing the SYNCHRONIZED clause does
                  not terminate at a natural boundary, is not included as part of the elementary
                  item. Such automatically generated FILLER positions are included in
                    ΓÇó   The size of any group item to which the FILLER item belongs
                    ΓÇó   The number of character positions allocated when the group item of which
                        the FILLER item is a part appears as the object of a REDEFINES clause
          9. The presence of the SYNCHRONIZED clause has no effect on the alignment of
             data items.

3.5.16. The USAGE Clause
        Function
        The USAGE clause specifies the format of a data item in the computer storage.

        General Format




        Syntax Rules
        1.   The USAGE clause can be written in any data description entry with a level number
             other than 66 or 88.
        2.   If the USAGE clause is written in the data description entry for a group item, it can
             also be written in the data description entry for any subordinate elementary item
             or group item, but the same usage must be specified in both entries.
        3.   An elementary data item, or an elementary data item subordinate to a group item,
             whose declaration contains a USAGE clause specifying BINARY,
             COMPUTATIONAL, or PACKED-DECIMAL must be declared with a PICTURE
             character string that describes a numeric item, that is, a PICTURE character string
             that contains only the symbols P, S, V, and 9 (see Section 3.5.11). An elementary
             data item, or an elementary data item subordinate to a group item whose
             declaration contains a USAGE specifying BINARY-1, must be declared with a
             PICTURE character string that describes an exact binary data item, that is, a
             PICTURE character string that contains only the symbols S and 1 (see Section
             3.5.11).
        4. COMP, COMP-1, COMP-2, COMP-4 and DISP are abbreviations for
           COMPUTATIONAL, COMPUTATIONAL-1, COMPUTATIONAL-2,
           COMPUTATIONAL-4, and DISPLAY, respectively.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                3ΓÇô47
Nucleus




          5.   An index data item can be referred to explicitly only in a SEARCH or SET
               statement, a relation condition, the USING phrase of a Procedure Division header,
               or the USING phrase of a CALL statement.
          6. The BLANK WHEN ZERO, JUSTIFIED, PICTURE, and VALUE clauses must not be
             specified for data items declared with the USAGE IS INDEX clause.
          7.   An elementary data item described with a USAGE IS INDEX clause must not be a
               conditional variable.
          8. COMPUTATIONAL-1 and COMPUTATIONAL-2 usage specifications cannot appear
             in a data description that has a PICTURE clause, because the computer storage
             format of these items is fixed.
          9. COMP-5 and COMPUTATIONAL-5 usage specification can appear only in data
             descriptions with a PICTURE clause of S9(4) or S9(9).
          10. Any data item whose declaration contains a USAGE DISP-I18N clause, must be an
              elementary item declared with a PICTURE character string that describes an
              alphabetic or alphanumeric item; that is, a PICTURE character string that contains
              only the symbols A or X. No editing characters are allowed in a PICTURE declared
              with USAGE DISP-I18N.
          11. Any data item whose declaration contains a USAGE BYTE-I18N must be an
              elementary data item declared with a PICTURE X(n).
          12. In the PROCEDURE DIVISION, POINTER data items can be explicitly referred to
              only when
               ΓÇó    named as input parameters through the USING clause of the PROCEDURE
                    DIVISION
               ΓÇó    used in a relation condition comparing for equal or not equal
               ΓÇó    moved to another POINTER item
               ΓÇó    used as the target or source in a format 5 SET statement
               ΓÇó    used as output parameters in the USING phrase of a CALL statement
               ΓÇó    displayed in a DISPLAY statement (the output format is octal).

          General Rules
          1.   If the USAGE clause is written at a group level, it applies to each elementary item
               in the group. The USAGE clause has the following meaning for a group item
               characters:
               a.   Any explicit usage for a group item applies to all the contained group or
                    elementary items.
               b. The group is always considered to be an alphanumeric string of ASCII




3ΓÇô48                                                                                 7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                                       Nucleus




        2.   The USAGE clause specifies the manner in which a data item is represented in the
             storage of a computer. It does not affect the use of the data item, although the
             specifications for some statements in the Procedure Division can restrict the
             USAGE clause of the operands referred to. The USAGE clause can affect the radix
             or type of character representation of the item. Table 3ΓÇô4 describes the meaning
             and internal representation of data. Table 3ΓÇô5 describes the alignment of data
             items by usage. Level 01 and level 77 data items are always aligned on word
             boundaries.
        3.   A COMPUTATIONAL, COMPUTATIONAL-1, or COMPUTATIONAL-2 item is capable
             of representing a value to be used in computations and must be numeric. If a
             group item is described as COMPUTATIONAL, COMPUTATIONAL-1, or
             COMPUTATIONAL-2, the elementary items in the group are COMPUTATIONAL,
             COMPUTATIONAL-1, or COMPUTATIONAL-2, respectively. The group item itself is
             not COMPUTATIONAL, COMPUTATIONAL-1, or COMPUTATIONAL-2. Such a group
             item cannot be used in computations.
        4. A BINARY, BINARY-1, or COMPUTATIONAL-4 item is capable of representing a
           value used in computations and must be numeric. If a group item is described as
           BINARY, BINARY-1, or COMPUTATIONAL-4, the elementary items in the group are
           BINARY, BINARY-1, or COMPUTATIONAL-4, respectively. The group item itself is
           not BINARY, BINARY-1, or COMPUTATIONAL-4. Such a group item cannot be used
           in computations.
        5.   The USAGE IS BINARY, BINARY-1, or COMPUTATIONAL-4 clause specifies that the
             data item is represented in the storage of the computer with a radix of 2.
        6. A PACKED-DECIMAL item is capable of representing a value used in computations
           and must be numeric. If a group item is described as PACKED-DECIMAL, the
           elementary items in the group are PACKED-DECIMAL. The group item itself is not
           PACKED-DECIMAL. Such a group item cannot be used in computations or in
           NUMERIC class condition tests.
        7.   The USAGE IS PACKED-DECIMAL clause specifies that the data item is
             represented in the storage of the computer with a radix of 10. PACKED-DECIMAL
             usage is equivalent to ASCII COBOL COMPUTATIONAL-3 usage (IBM OS/360
             allocation).
        8. The USAGE IS DISPLAY clause (whether specified explicitly or implicitly) specifies
           that a standard data format is used to represent a data item in the storage of the
           computer and that the data item is aligned on a character boundary.
        9. If the USAGE clause is not specified for an elementary item or for any group to
           which the item belongs, the usage is implicitly DISPLAY.
        10. The USAGE IS INDEX clause specifies that a data item is an index data item and
            contains a value that must correspond to an occurrence number of a table
            element. If a group item is described with the USAGE IS INDEX clause, the
            elementary items in the group are all index data items. The group itself is not an
            index data item and must not be used in the SEARCH or SET statement or in a
            relation condition, but can be referenced in the USING phrase either of a CALL
            statement or of the programΓÇÖs Procedure Division header.
        11. When a MOVE statement or an input-output statement that references a group
            item that contains an index data item is executed, no conversion of the index data
            item takes place.

Nucleus




          12. A COMPUTATIONAL-5 item depending on its picture declaration is capable of
              representing a half-word or full-word binary signed numeric value to be used in
              computations. Its main purpose is parameter passing between COBOL and C
              programs.
          13. Whenever a data item described with USAGE DISP-I18N is explicitly used in a
              comparison (that is, IF, EVALUATE, or SEARCH), that comparison is done in a
              culturally sensitive manner (that is, the comparison is done based on the locale
              (LC_COLLATE) that is in force at the time the comparison is done). All other uses
              of data items declared as DISP-I18N are the same as if they had been declared as
              USAGE DISPLAY.
          14. When a BYTE-I18N data item is used in a comparison, the data item is treated as a
              bit string and no conversion is done. For comparison of different lengths, the
              shorter item is padded with binary zeros on the right. A data item defined as BYTE-
              I18N can be the receiver in a MOVE statement only if the sender is another BYTE-
              I18N data item or one of the figurative constants LOW-VALUES or HIGH-VALUES.
              A BYTE-I18N data item can be the sender in a MOVE statement only if the receiver
              is also a BYTE-I18N data item. A data item described as BYTE-I18N is used to hold
              the results of a call to the string_transform I18NLIB service routine. Data items
              declared as BYTE-I18N cannot be used in any arithmetic or string manipulation
              statements.

          15. If a group item is described with the USAGE IS POINTER clause, the elementary
              items within the group are pointer data items; the group itself is an alphanumeric
              group (not a pointer data item) and cannot be used in the syntax where a pointer
              data item is allowed.
             Pointer data items can be part of an alphanumeric group that is referred to in a
             MOVE statement or an input/output statement. However, if a pointer data item is
             part of a group, there is no conversion of values when the statement is executed.
             A pointer data item cannot be a conditional variable.
             A pointer data item does not belong to any class or category.
             The JUSTIFIED, PICTURE, and BLANK WHEN ZERO clauses cannot be used to
             describe group or elementary items defined with the USAGE IS POINTER clause.
             USAGE of POINTER is implied for the ADDRESS OF phrase.

        The alignment of an elementary exact binary data item is determined by the following
        rules:

        1.   If the current data item is the first elementary data item in a group, the current
             data item is aligned on the same character boundary as the group item.
        2.   If the current data item is the first data item following the last data item of a
             group, the current data item is aligned on a character boundary.
        3.   If the preceding elementary data item is not an exact binary data item, the current
             data item is aligned on a character boundary.
        4. If the preceding elementary data item is an exact binary data item and none of the
           above rules applies, the current data item is aligned on the bit following the
           preceding data item.

3.5.17. The VALUE Clause
        Function
        The VALUE clause defines the initial values of Common-Storage Section and
        Working-Storage Section data names, and the values associated with condition
        names.

        Format 1




        Format 2




        Syntax Rules
        1.   The words THRU and THROUGH are equivalent.
        2.   A signed numeric literal must have associated with it a signed numeric PICTURE
             character string.
        3.   All numeric literals in a VALUE clause of an item must have a value within the
             range of values indicated by the PICTURE clause, and must not have a value that
             would require truncation of nonzero digits. Nonnumeric literals in a VALUE clause
             of an item must not exceed the size indicated by the PICTURE clause.
        4. The VALUE clause must not be specified in any entry that is part of the description
           or redefinition of an external data record. The VALUE clause must be specified for
           condition name entries associated with such data description entries.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                    3ΓÇô53
Nucleus




          General Rules
          The VALUE clause must not conflict with other clauses in the data description of the
          item or in the data description within the hierarchy of the item. The following rules
          apply:

          1.   If the category of the item is numeric, all literals in the VALUE clause must be
               numeric. If the literal defines the value of a working storage item, the literal is
               aligned in the data item according to the standard alignment rules. (See Section
               2.4.19)
          2.   If the category of the item is alphabetic, alphanumeric, alphanumeric edited, or
               numeric edited, all literals in the VALUE clause must be nonnumeric literals. The
               literal is aligned in the data item as if the data item had been described as
               alphanumeric. (See Section 2.4.19.) Editing characters in the PICTURE clause are
               included in determining the size of the data item but have no effect on initialization
               of the data item. (See Section 3.5.11) Therefore, the VALUE for an edited item must
               be specified in an edited form.
          3.   Initialization is not affected by any BLANK WHEN ZERO or JUSTIFIED clause that
               can be specified.

Condition-Name Rules

          1.   In a condition-name entry, the VALUE clause is required. The VALUE clause and the
               condition name itself are the only two clauses permitted in the entry. The
               characteristics of a condition name are implicitly those of its conditional variable.
          2.   Format 2 can be used only in connection with condition names. (See Section 2.4.7)
               Wherever the THRU phrase is used, literal-2 must be less than literal-3.

Data Description Entries Other Than Condition Names
          1.   Rules governing the use of the VALUE clause differ with the respective sections
               of the Data Division:
               a.   In level 1, the VALUE clause cannot be used in the File Section. In the File
                    Section, the VALUE clause can be used only in condition-name entries;
                    therefore, the initial value of the data items in the File Section is undefined.
               b. In level 1, the VALUE clause cannot be used in the Linkage Section. In the
                  Linkage Section, the VALUE clause can be used only in condition-name entries.
               c.   In the Working-Storage Section and the Common-Storage Section, the VALUE
                    clause must be used in condition-name entries. VALUE clauses in the
                    Working-Storage and Common-Storage Sections of a program take effect only
                    when the program is placed into its initial state. If the VALUE clause is used in
                    the description of the data item, the data item is initialized to the defined
                    value. If the VALUE clause is not associated with a data item, the initial value of
                    that data item is undefined.
          2.   The VALUE clause must not be stated in a data description entry that contains a
               REDEFINES clause or in an entry that is subordinate to an entry containing a
               REDEFINES clause. This rule does not apply to condition-name entries.




3ΓÇô54                                                                                    7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                                           Nucleus




        3.   If the VALUE clause is used in an entry at the group level, the literal must be a
             figurative constant or a nonnumeric literal, and the group area is initialized without
             consideration for the individual elementary or group items contained within this
             group. The VALUE clause cannot be stated at the subordinate levels within this
             group.
        4. The VALUE clause must not be specified for a group item containing items
           subordinate to it with descriptions including JUSTIFIED, SYNCHRONIZED, or
           USAGE (other than USAGE IS DISPLAY).
        5.   If a VALUE clause is specified in a data description entry of a data item that is
             associated with a variable occurrence data item, the initialization of the data item
             behaves as if the value of the data item referenced by the DEPENDING ON phrase
             in the OCCURS clause specified for the variable occurrence data item is set to the
             maximum number of occurrences as specified by that OCCURS clause. A data
             item is associated with a variable occurrence data item in any of the following
             cases:
             a.   It is a group data item that contains a variable occurrence data item.
             b. It is a variable occurrence data item.
             c.   It is a data item that is subordinate to a variable occurrence data item.
             If a VAL UE clause is associated with the data item referenced by a DEPENDING
             ON phrase, that value is considered to be placed in the data item after the variable
             occurrence data item is initialized. (See Section 3.5.10.)
        6. A format 1 VALUE clause specified in a data description entry that contains an
           OCCURS clause or in an entry that is subordinate to an OCCURS clause causes
           every occurrence of the associated data item to be assigned the specified value.
        7.   A VALUE clause associated with a data item declared as USAGE BYTE-I18N can
             only refer to the figurative constants HIGH-VALUES or LOW-VALUES.
        8. A VALUE clause associated with a data item declared as USAGE POINTER can only
           refer to the figurative constants NULL or NULLS.

3.5.18. The USING POINTER Clause
        The USING POINTER clause permits the implicit basing of a data item. The data item is
        based upon the address that is pointed by the USING POINTER data item.

        General Format
             USING POINTER data-name-4

        Syntax Rules
        1.   The USING POINTER clause can only be specified with an 01/77 level item declared
             in the Working-Storage Section.
        2.   data-name-4 must be an elementary item defined as 1(36) BINARY-1.
        3.   data-name-4 might be defined in Working-Storage, Common-Storage, or Linkage.
        4. VALUE clauses must not be specified for the data item associated with the USING
           POINTER clause.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                 3ΓÇô55
Nucleus




          5.   VALUE clauses must not be specified for any item subordinate to the data item
               associated with the USING POINTER clause.
          6. The EXTERNAL clause must not be specified for the data item associated with the
             USING POINTER clause.
          7.   The USING POINTER data-name-4 clause cannot be specified in the same
               declaration as a REDEFINES.
          8. The data item that contains the USING POINTER data-name-4 clause must not be
             specified in an APPLY EXREF/EXDEF clause.

          General Rules
          1.   It is the userΓÇÖs responsibility to assign a value to data-name-4 (virtual address)
               before referencing the data item associated with the USING POINTER clause or
               any item subordinate to it. This can be accomplished by using the LOC$,
               UCOBMALLOC$, UCOBCALLOC$ or UCOBREALLOC$ service routine or by passing
               the value into the program. See Volume 2 for further details. The contents of
               data-name-4 must be a full Virtual Address (VA) pointing to a whole word (a word
               pointer).
          2.   Arithmetic operations can be performed on data-name-4, but the user must be
               careful to ensure that data-name-4 contains a valid address. Note that adding a
               value of 1 to data-name-4 results in pointing to the next word.
          3.   data-name-4 can be associated with multiple 01 level items.

          Example 1
                     working-storage section.

                     01   ptr1 pic 1(36) binary-1.

                     01   baseditem USING POINTER ptr1 pic xxxx.

                     01   buffer1 pic xxxx value 'ABCD'.

                     01   buffer2 pic xxxx value 'WXYZ'.

                     procedure division.

                     begin.

                    * Get the address of buffer1 and place it into ptr1, then display

                    * the value in the based item.

                          call 'loc$' using buffer1 ptr1.

                          display baseditem.

                       * Change the value of buffer1 and redisplay the value in the
                         based item




3ΓÇô56                                                                              7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                              Nucleus




                          move 'JKLM' to buffer1.

                          display baseditem.

                  * Get the address of buffer2 and place it into ptr1, then display

                  * the value in the based item.

                          call 'loc$' using buffer2 ptr1.

                          display baseditem.

           The result of executing the above code segment will be

           ABCD

           JKLM

           WXYZ

        Example 2
                   WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.

                   01 buf USING POINTER addrname1.

                          02 bfgp OCCURS 1 TO 1000 DEPENDING ON bufsize.

                            03 bfchar PIC 1(9) BINARY-1.

                   01 bufsize PIC s9(10) BINARY VALUE 1000.

                   01 retstat       PIC 1(36) BINARY-1 VALUE 0.

                   01 addrname1 PIC 1(36) BINARY-1.

                   01 i      PIC 9(10) BINARY VALUE 0.

                   procedure division.

                   pppp.

                  *Allocate buf

                           CALL 'UCOBMALLOC$' USING bufsize, addrname1, retstat.

                               MOVE i TO bfchar (i)

3.5.19. USAGE POINTER pointers
          Pointer handling allows for UCS COBOL to be compatible with IBM COBOL pointers
          and based storage. UCOB has two separate mechanisms for defining based storage
          and two kinds of pointers. One approach involves the USING POINTER clause and the
          other instance is the USAGE POINTER clause.

          The USING POINTER clause is used on 01 level declarations in the
          WORKING-STORAGE SECTION to define a based item and the pointer it is based on.
          The pointers hold a one-word VA address defined in Section 3.5.18 The USING
          POINTER clause.

          The USAGE POINTER clause is used on a data item for a based structure in the Linkage
          Section. Use the SET statement to base a Linkage Section 01/77 data item. Precede
          the data name with the ADDRESS OF phrase and populate with either the ADDRESS
          OF another structure or variable (at any level) or to a pointer that was declared as
          USAGE POINTER. This pointer form has byte granularity and can point at byte
          boundaries. In order to access items on byte boundaries, the UCS C two-word pointer
          form is used for the pointers. (They are compatible with UCS C pointers.) Arithmetic
          on these C-style pointers is not allowed since it would produce invalid results (adding
          1 to one of these pointers would NOT cause it to point at the next byte).




3ΓÇô58                                                                             7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                                        Nucleus




Loading an Address of a Data Item

        There are three methods available to load a USAGE POINTER data item. The first
        method involves using a call to LOC$. The second argument of the call to LOC$ must
        be declared as USAGE POINTER in order to receive a pointer address.

        For example:

            CALL 'LOC$' USING data-item         usage-pointer-item.

        data-item              Any elementary or group item declared at 01/77 level
        usage-pointer-item     A USAGE POINTER data item


        The second method involves using a SET statement to load a pointer data with the
        address of another data item. The SET statement requires use of the ADDRESS OF
        phrase to obtain a pointer.

        For example:

            SET pointer-name TO ADDRESS OF data-item

        data-item              Any elementary or group item declared at any level
        pointer-name           A USAGE POINTER data item


        The third method involves calling UCOBMALLOC$2 to get new storage, defined in
        Volume 2, Section 10.25.5).

        For example:

            CALL 'UCOBMALLOC$2' USING number-of-bytes, address-name, return-status

        number-of-bytes      is an integer variable. Define number-of-bytes as PIC 1(36)
                             BINARY-1
        address-name         is a USAGE POINTER variable
        return-status        is an integer variable. Define return-status as PIC 1(36) BINARY-1

Basing Data Items
        Data items declared in the Linkage Section can be based on other data items or
        pointers. The following must be true to base a Linkage Section data item:

        ΓÇó    The Linkage Section structure or data item must be at the 01/77 level
        ΓÇó    There must be at least one SET ADDRESS OF <data-item> statement in the
             PROCEDURE division to give it an address
        ΓÇó    Note that a based Linkage Section data item may or may not also be a parameter
             to the PROCEDURE (specified in the USING clause)




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                3ΓÇô59
Nucleus




          An internal implicit pointer is created and the entire 01/77 data item can be based on
          the address of another structure. Any 01/77 Linkage Section item not in the
          PROCEDURE USING clause is a BASED item, whether its address is SET or not. Note
          that you must ensure that the storage you are basing a structure on is large enough to
          encompass the extent of the structure. The compiler cannot check this for you. If the
          structure exceeds the storage size, you will reference data meant for other variables
          and could overwrite them, giving unknown (but incorrect) results.

              SET ADDRESS OF data-name TO usage-pointer-item

          Note: Runtime failures can occur if an invalid address is accessed.

Setting the Address of Linkage Section Items
          Generally, when one UCOB program calls another, operands are passed from the
          calling UCOB program to the subprogram in the following manner:

          ΓÇó    The calling program uses the CALL USING statement to pass operands to the
               called program, and
          ΓÇó    The called program specifies the USING phrase in the Procedure Division header.

          For each operand that is listed on the CALL USING statement in the calling program,
          there must be a corresponding operand that is specified by the USING phrase in the
          Procedure Division of the called program.

          When using the ADDRESS OF phrase, you no longer need to ensure a one-to-one
          mapping between the USING phrases of two programs. For those data items in the
          Linkage Section that are not specified in the USING phrase of the Procedure Division
          header, you can use a SET statement to specify the starting address of the data
          structure. Once the SET statement is executed, the data item can be freely referenced
          after the address of the data item is set. You can also SET the ADDRESS OF a Linkage
          Section data item that is a parameter to the routine (specified in the USING clause).
          This moves references to the parameter data item from the original callerΓÇÖs storage to
          the new location.

Initializing and Comparing Pointers using the NULL Constant
          The NULL figurative constant represents a two-word value of binary zeroes. It can be
          used in place of a USAGE POINTER data item in executable statements to represent a
          null or void pointer value. For example:

                     WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
                     77 APTR USAGE POINTER VALUE NULL.
                     LINKAGE SECTION.
                     01 AGRP PIC X(9).
                     PROCEDURE DIVISION.
                         SET ADDRESS OF AGRP TO NULL.
                         IF APTR = NULL THEN
                            DISPLAY 'APTR IS NULL'
                         END-IF.




3ΓÇô60                                                                             7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                                  Nucleus




        In the above example, pointer APTR is set to NULL in the Working-Storage section.
        The comparison in the procedure division will be TRUE and the DISPLAY statement is
        executed. Note that only the EQUAL and NOT EQUAL operators are allowed as
        relational operators with USAGE POINTER pointers. Also, pointers can only be
        compared to other pointers or to NULL.

3.6. Procedure Division
        This subsection describes the Procedure Division and its associated arithmetic
        expressions.

3.6.1. General Description
        The Procedure Division contains procedures to be executed by the object program.
        The Procedure Division is optional in a COBOL source program.

        The general formats of the Procedure Division in the Nucleus are shown below.

        Format 1
           PROCEDURE DIVISON.

           {section-name SECTION.

           [paragraph-name.

            [sentence]...]...}...



        Format 2
           PROCEDURE DIVISON.

           [paragraph-name.

            [sentence]...]...}...

3.6.2. Arithmetic Expressions
        This subsection defines an arithmetic expression and identifies available arithmetic
        operators.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                              3ΓÇô69
Nucleus




Definition of an Arithmetic Expression
          An arithmetic expression can be an identifier of a numeric elementary item; a numeric
          literal; the figurative constant ZERO (ZEROS, ZEROES), such identifiers, figurative
          constants, and literals separated by arithmetic operators; two arithmetic expressions
          separated by an arithmetic operator; or an arithmetic expression enclosed in
          parentheses. Any arithmetic expression can be preceded by a unary operator.

          The permissible combinations of variables, numeric literals, arithmetic operators, and
          parentheses are given in Table 3ΓÇô6, ΓÇ£Combination of Symbols in Arithmetic
          ExpressionsΓÇ¥.

          Those identifiers and literals appearing in an arithmetic expression must represent
          either numeric elementary items or numeric literals on which arithmetic can be
          performed.

Arithmetic Operators
          There are five binary arithmetic operators and two unary arithmetic operators that can
          be used in arithmetic expressions. They are represented by specific characters that
          must be preceded by a space and followed by a space.


                  Binary Arithmetic                       Meaning
                      Operators

                          +                                Addition
                          -                              Subtraction
                          *                             Multiplication
                          /                                Division
                         **                            Exponentiation



                  Unary Arithmetic                        Meaning
                     Operators

                          +              The effect of multiplication by numeric
                                         literals +1
                          -              The effect of multiplication by numeric
                                         literals -1




3ΓÇô70                                                                               7831 0448ΓÇô005
                                                                                         Nucleus




Formation and Evaluation Rules
        1.     Parentheses can be used in arithmetic expressions to specify the order in which
               elements are to be evaluated. Expressions within parentheses are evaluated first,
               and, within nested parentheses, evaluation proceeds from the least inclusive set
               to the most inclusive set. When parentheses are not used, or parenthesized
               expressions are at the same level of inclusiveness, the following hierarchical order
               of execution is implied:
                        1st = Unary plus and minus
                        2nd = Exponentiation
                        3rd = Multiplication and division
                        4th = Addition and subtraction
        2.     Parentheses are used either to eliminate ambiguities in logic where consecutive
               operations of the same hierarchical level appear, or to modify the normal
               hierarchical sequence of execution in expressions where it is necessary to have
               some deviation from the normal precedence. When the sequence of execution is
               not specified by parentheses, the order of execution of consecutive operations of
               the same hierarchical level is from left to right.
        3.     The ways in which identifiers, literals, operators, and parentheses can be
               combined in an arithmetic expression are summarized in Table 3ΓÇô6, where
               a.       The letter P indicates a permissible pair of symbols.
               b. The character - indicates an invalid pair.

                    Table 3ΓÇô6. Combination of Symbols in Arithmetic Expressions


          First Symbol                                         Second Symbol

                                Identifier or     + - * / **    Unary + or -    (           )
                                   Literal

             Identifier or            -               P              -          -           P
                literal
              + - * / **              P               -              P          P           -
             Unary + or -             P               -              -          P           -
                    (                 P               -              P          P           -
                    )                 -               P              -          -           P


        4. An arithmetic expression can begin only with the symbol ( , +, -, an identifier, or a
           literal and can end only with a ), an identifier, or a literal. There must be a
           one-to-one correspondence between left and right parentheses of an arithmetic
           expression such that each left parenthesis is to the left of its corresponding right
           parenthesis. If the first operator in an arithmetic expression is a unary operator, it
           must be immediately preceded by a left parenthesis if that arithmetic expression
           immediately follows an identifier or another arithmetic expression.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                   3ΓÇô71
Nucleus




          5.    The following rules apply to evaluation of exponentiation in an arithmetic
                expression:
                a.   If the value of an expression to be raised to a power is zero, the exponent
                     must have a value greater than zero. Otherwise, the size error condition
                     exists. (See Section 3.6.5.)
                b. If the evaluation yields both a positive and a negative real number, the value
                   returned as the result is the positive number.
                c.   If no real number exists as the result of the evaluation, the size error condition
                     exists.
          6. Arithmetic expressions allow the user to combine arithmetic operations without
             the restrictions on composite of operands or receiving data items. See, for
             example, syntax rule 3, in Section 3.6.7.

          The following examples illustrate natural and parentheses-enforced ordering of
          COBOL arithmetic expressions. In these examples, let A = 4, B = 6, C = 2, D = 3, and E
          = 12.


                               Expression             Evaluation

                      A + B * C ** D             52
                      A+B*C                      16
                      E-A/C                      10

3.6.3. Conditional Expressions
        Conditional expressions identify conditions that are tested to enable the object
        program to select between alternate paths of control, depending on the truth value of
        the condition. A conditional expression has a truth value of true or false. Conditional
        expressions are specified in the EVALUATE, IF, PERFORM, and SEARCH statements.
        Two categories of conditions are associated with conditional expressions: simple and
        complex. Each category can be enclosed within any number of paired parentheses, in
        which case its category is not changed.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                             3ΓÇô73
Nucleus




Simple Conditions
          The simple conditions are the relation, class, condition name, switch-status, and sign
          conditions. A simple condition has a truth value of true or false. The inclusion in
          parentheses of simple conditions does not change the simple condition truth value.

          Relation Condition
          A relation condition causes a comparison of two operands, each of which can be the
          data item referenced by an identifier, a literal, the value resulting from an arithmetic
          expression, or an index name. A relation condition has a truth value of true if the
          relation exists between the operands. Comparison of two numeric operands is
          permitted regardless of the formats specified in their respective USAGE clauses.
          However, for all other comparisons, the operands must have the same usage. If either
          of the operands is a group item, the nonnumeric comparison rules apply.

          The format of a relation condition is




          The first operand (identifier-1, literal-1, arithmetic-expression-1, or index-name-1) is
          called the subject of the condition; the second operand (identifier-2, literal-2,
          arithmetic-expression-2, or index-name-2) is called the object of the condition. The
          relation condition must contain at least one reference to a variable.

          The relational operators specify the type of comparison to be made in a relation
          condition. A space must precede and follow each reserved word comprising the
          relational operator. When used, NOT and the next keyword or relation character are
          one relational operator that defines the comparison to be executed for truth value.
          The following relational operators are equivalent: IS NOT GREATER THAN is equivalent
          to IS LESS THAN OR EQUAL TO; IS NOT LESS THAN is equivalent to IS GREATER
          THAN OR EQUAL TO.

                            Meaning                                Relational Operator

         Greater than or not greater than           IS [ NOT ] GREATER THAN
                                                    IS [ NOT ] >
         Less than or not less than                 IS [ NOT ] LESS THAN
                                                    IS [ NOT ] <
         Equal to or not equal to                   IS [ NOT ] EQUAL TO
                                                    IS [ NOT ] =
         Greater than or equal to                   IS GREATER THAN OR EQUAL TO
                                                    IS >=
         Less than or equal to                      IS LESS THAN OR EQUAL TO
                                                    IS <=
        Comparison of Numeric Operands
        For operands whose class is numeric (see Section 2.4.17) a comparison is made with
        respect to the algebraic value of the operands. The length of the literal or arithmetic
        expression operands, in terms of the number of digits represented, is not significant.
        Zero is considered a unique value regardless of the sign.

        Comparison of these operands is permitted regardless of the manner in which their
        usage is described. Unsigned numeric operands are considered positive for purposes
        of comparison.

        Comparison of COMPUTATIONAL-1 and COMPUTATIONAL-2 operands with
        nonfloating-point operands might not always be valid. Since COMPUTATIONAL-1 and
        COMPUTATIONAL-2 operands are floating-point and binary-scaled, a loss of decimal
        precision might occur during arithmetic operations. This loss of decimal precision
        might result in invalid comparisons between COMPUTATIONAL-1 and
        COMPUTATIONAL-2 operands and decimal operands.

        Comparison of Nonnumeric Operands
        For nonnumeric DISPLAY operands, or one numeric DISPLAY and one nonnumeric
        DISPLAY operand, a comparison is made with respect to a specified collating
        sequence of characters. (See Section 3.4.4.) If one of the operands is specified as
        numeric, it must be an integer data item or an integer literal and:

        1.   If the nonnumeric operand is an elementary data item or nonnumeric literal, the
             numeric operand is treated as though it were moved to an elementary
             alphanumeric data item of the same size as the numeric data item (in terms of
             standard data format characters), and the contents of this alphanumeric data item
             were then compared to the nonnumeric operand. (See Section 3.6.19 and Section
             3.5.11.)




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                 3ΓÇô75
Nucleus




          2.    If the nonnumeric operand is a group item, the numeric operand is treated as
                though it were moved to a group item of the same size as the numeric data item
                (in terms of standard data format characters), and the contents of this group item
                were then compared to the nonnumeric operand. (See Section 3.6.19 and Section
                3.5.11.)
          3.    A noninteger numeric operand cannot be compared to a nonnumeric operand. The
                size of an operand is the total number of standard data format characters in the
                operand. Numeric and nonnumeric operands can be compared only when their
                usage is the same.

          Comparison of Equal and Unequal Operand Sizes
          There are two cases to consider: operands of equal size and operands of unequal size.

          1.    Operands of equal size
                If the operands are of equal size, comparison involves characters in corresponding
                character positions starting from the high order end and continuing until either a
                pair of unequal characters is encountered or the low order end of the operand is
                reached, whichever comes first. The operands are determined to be equal if all
                pairs of corresponding characters are equal.
                The first encountered pair of unequal characters is compared to determine their
                relative position in the collating sequence. The operand that contains the character
                that is positioned higher in the collating sequence is considered to be the greater
                operand.
          2.    Operands of unequal size
                If the operands are of unequal size, comparison proceeds as though the shorter
                operand were extended on the right by enough spaces to make the operands of
                equal size.

          The following example shows the effect of a collating sequence on alphanumeric
          comparisons:

               ALPHABET.
               SPECIAL-NAMES.

                 ALPHABET NEW-ALPHABET IS "A" "B" "CDE" "F" ALSO "f" 72 THRU "U"
                 "Z" THRU "V" "0" THRU 58.
                 .
                 .
                 .
               DATA DIVISION.
               WORKING-STORAGE SECTION.
               01 DATA-NAMES.
                 02 DATA-NAME1 PIC XXX VALUE 'FFF'.
                 02 DATA-NAME2 PIC XXX VALUE 'fff'.

        Comparisons Involving Index Names and Index Data Items
        Relation tests can be made only between

        1.   Two index names. The result is the same as if the corresponding occurrence
             numbers were compared.
        2.    An index name and a data item (other than an index data item) or literal. The
             occurrence number that corresponds to the value of the index name is compared
             to the data item or literal.
        3.   An index data item and an index name or another index data item. The actual
             values are compared without conversion.

        Comparisons Involving Culturally Sensitive Data Items
        If either of the operands involved in the comparison are described as USAGE DISP-
        I18N, then the comparison is done based on the locale (LC_COLLATE) that is currently
        active. This comparison results in a call to the internationalization service routine
        string_collate.

        If both operands that are explicitly specified in a comparison are described as USAGE
        BYTE-I18N, they are compared (left aligned) as bit strings with no conversions taking
        place. If the operands are of unequal lengths, binary zero padding is done on the right
        of the shorter operand. No reference modification can be specified on BYTE-I18N data
        items being compared.

        Class Condition
        The class condition determines whether the operand is numeric, alphabetic,
        alphabetic-lower, alphabetic-upper, or contains only the characters in the set of
        characters specified by the CLASS clause as defined in the SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph
        of the Environment Division. The class of an operand is determined as follows:

        1.   An operand is numeric if it consists entirely of the characters 0, 1, 2, 3, ..., 9, with
             or without an operational sign.
        2.   An operand is alphabetic if it consists entirely of the uppercase letters A through
             Z, space, or the lowercase letters a through z, space, or any combination of the
             uppercase and lowercase letters and spaces.
        3.   An operand is alphabetic lower if it consists entirely of the lowercase letters a
             through z and space.
        4. An operand is alphabetic upper if it consists entirely of the uppercase letters A
           through Z and space.
        5.   An operand is in conformance to class name if it consists entirely of the
             characters listed in the definition of class name in the SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph.




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                     3ΓÇô79
Nucleus




          The general format of the class condition is




          The identifier being tested must reference a data item whose usage is explicitly or
          implicitly DISPLAY or DISP-I18N. DISP-I18N items are treated the same as items
          declared with USAGE DISPLAY. If the identifier is a function identifier, it must
          reference an alphanumeric function. The NUMERIC test can also be used on an
          elementary item with usage PACKED-DECIMAL.

          When used, NOT and the next keyword specify one class condition that defines the
          class test to be executed for truth value; for example, NOT NUMERIC is a truth test
          for determining that an operand is nonnumeric.

          The NUMERIC test cannot be used with an item whose data description describes the
          item as alphabetic or as a group item composed of elementary items whose data
          description indicates the presence of operational signs. If the data description of the
          item being tested does not indicate the presence of an operational sign, the item
          being tested is determined to be numeric only if the contents are numeric and an
          operational sign is not present. If the data description of the item does indicate the
          presence of an operational sign, the item being tested is determined to be numeric
          only if the contents are numeric and a valid operational sign is present. Valid
          operational signs for data items described with the SIGN IS SEPARATE clause are the
          standard data format characters, plus (+) and minus (-). See Table 3ΓÇô1 for what
          constitutes valid signs for data items not described with the SIGN IS SEPARATE
          clause. For signed or unsigned PACKED-DECIMAL fields, the valid operational signs are
          +, - , or ΓÇ£unsigned.ΓÇ¥

          The ALPHABETIC test cannot be used with an item whose data description describes
          the item as numeric. The result of the test is true if the contents of the data item
          referenced by identifier consist entirely of alphabetic characters.

          The ALPHABETIC-LOWER test cannot be used with an item whose data description
          describes the item as numeric. The result of the test is true if the content of the data
          item referred to by identifier consists entirely of the lowercase alphabetic characters
          a through z and the space.

          The ALPHABETIC-UPPER test cannot be used with an item whose data description
          describes the item as numeric. The result of the test is true if the content of the data
          item referred to by identifier consists entirely of the uppercase alphabetic characters
          A through Z and the space.

          The class name test must not be used with an item whose data description describes
          the item as numeric.

        Condition-Name Condition (Conditional Variable)
        In a condition-name condition, a conditional variable is tested to determine whether or
        not its value is equal to one of the values associated with condition-name-1. The
        general format for the condition name condition is

           condition-name-1

        If condition-name-1 is associated with a range or ranges of values, then the
        conditional variable is tested to determine whether or not its value falls in this range,
        including the end values.

        The rules for comparing a conditional variable with a condition-name value are the
        same as those specified for relation conditions.

        The result of the test is true if one of the values corresponding to condition-name-1
        equals the value of its associated conditional variable.

        The following example represents the data description for conditional valiable
        MARITAL-STATUS:

           02 MARITAL-STATUS PICTURE IS 9.
               88 SINGLE VALUE IS 1.
               88 MARRIED VALUE IS 2.
               88 DIVORCED VALUE IS 3.
               88 WIDOWED VALUE IS 4.
               88 EVER-MARRIED VALUE 2 THRU 4.

        Using an IF statement, the test to determine marital status can appear as

           IF MARRIED . . .

        which is equivalent to

           IF MARITAL-STATUS IS EQUAL TO 2 . . .

        Again, as in the relational condition, NOT is used to specify the opposite of what the
        condition-name test would normally specify. So, for example

           IF NOT SINGLE . . .

        is equivalent to

           IF MARITAL-STATUS IS NOT EQUAL TO 1 . . .




7831 0448ΓÇô005                                                                                 3ΓÇô81
Nucleus




          The same situation could be checked by writing

            IF EVER-MARRIED . . .

          which is equivalent to

            IF MARITAL-STATUS NOT < 2 AND
              MARITAL-STATUS NOT > 4 . . .

          When a single condition name is associated with a list of values or range of values, a
          programmer can express what is equivalent to rather complex compound relationals
          in a simple condition-name condition.

          The following example defines the code names for various bolts in inventory:

            03 PART-NUMBER PIC X(5).
                88 BOLT VALUE IS "AA000" THRU
                  "AA999", "AX010" THRU "AZ999",
                   "P1000", "P1010".

          Using the IF statement to determine whether a part is a bolt, a programmer can write

            IF BOLT GO TO IS-BOLT.

          which is equivalent to writing

            IF PART-NUMBER NOT < "AA000" AND
                  PART-NUMBER NOT > "AA999" OR
                  PART-NUMBER NOT < "AX010" AND
                  PART-NUMBER NOT > "AZ999" OR
                  PART-NUMBER = "P1000" OR "P1010"
                  GO TO IS-BOLT .

          Switch-Status Condition
          A switch-status condition determines the on or off status of an implementor-defined
          switch. The implementor name and the on or off value associated with the condition
          must be named in the SPECIAL-NAMES paragraph of the Environment Division.

          The general format for the switch-status condition is

            condition-name.

          The result of the test is true if the switch is set to the specified position
          corresponding to condition-name.

          The implementor names SWITCH-13, SWITCH-14, . . . , SWITCH-24 correspond to the
          bits in the last third of the condition word set by the SET mnemonic-name statement.
          Therefore, SWITCH-13 is bit 11, SWITCH-14 is bit 10, . . . , SWITCH-24 is bit 0. The
          switch-status condition ON checks for a 1 in the appropriate bit; OFF checks for a 0.

        The implementor names SWITCH-1, SWITCH-2, . . . , SWITCH-12 correspond to the bits
        in the middle or second third of the condition word set by the @SETC command
        statement. Therefore, SWITCH-1 is bit 23, SWITCH-2 is bit 22, . . . , SWITCH-12 is bit 12.
        The switch-status condition ON checks for a 1 in the appropriate bit, OFF checks for a
        0.

        The following example sets SWITCH-6, SWITCH-7, SWITCH-9, SWITCH-11, and
        SWITCH-12 on; other switches are off.

           @SETC       153/T2

        Sign Condition
        The sign condition determines whether or not the algebraic value of an arithmetic
        expression is less than, greater than, or equal to zero. The general format for a sign
        condition is




        NOT, when used, and the next keyword specify one sign condition that defines the
        algebraic test to be executed for truth value; for example, NOT ZERO is a truth test for
        a nonzero (positive or negative) value. An operand is positive, if its value is greater
        than zero, negative if its value is less than zero, and zero if its value is equal to zero.
        The zero test will be true for any numeric item containing a zero even if the field
        contains a positive or negative operational sign. The arithmetic expression must
        contain at least one reference to a variable.
